text:
Luxembourg on Tuesday unveiled plans to work together with Germany and Austria to accelerate the market roll-out of renewable electricity-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel, (eSAF) in Europe, dedicating €60 million to the project.

The three countries are launching what they described as a “dual auction mechanism” that is aimed at offering producers long-term revenue certainty and providing buyers with competitive, short-term contracts. Government funding will be available to bridge any price gaps between the two sides.

Austria, like Luxembourg, is budgeting €60 million for the project, while Germany is providing up to €2 billion, according to a press release issued on Tuesday.

‘Temporal and economic gap’

“There is currently a structural problem,” the Luxembourg government press release stated. While producers need long-term off-take agreements to underpin their investment decisions, buyers typically enter into contracts for aviation fuels over significantly shorter timeframes, the government said.

“This temporal and economic gap has so far hampered the construction of new production facilities. This is precisely where the dual-auction mechanism comes into play,” the press statement read. By acting as an intermediary to bridge the gap between the supply and demand prices using government subsidies, long-term production prospects can be linked to competitive supply terms the government claimed.

The aim is to facilitate investment decisions for new eSAF production facilities whilst simultaneously developing a competitive market for the purchase of the fuel. The support programme is subject to approval under state aid law. But the European Commission already last December supported the launch of the eSAF Early Movers’ Coalition, which aims to scale up the production and uptake of synthetic aviation fuels.

Also read:

Construction on Findel airport’s new €100m fuel farm gets underway

Early movers’ coalition

Luxembourg, Austria and Germany were founding members of the eSAF Early Movers’ Coalition - alongside France, Finland, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain.

Luxembourg’s economy minister Lex Delles said that the joint initiative marked the three countries as “pioneers” on a path that will not only see them protect the climate, “but also seek to promote industrial value creation in Europe and our independence from fossil fuel imports.”

Mobility minister Yuriko Backes said that the new initiative will support the expansion of eSAF production and accelerate their EU-wide market introduction. “Luxembourg is playing an active role in building a safe, sustainable and competitive aviation sector by promoting new production capacities and helping to ensure that part of this production is available to our domestic market,” Backes added.

“With this clear vision for the future, we are laying the foundations today for the sustainable mobility of tomorrow, which will both meet the demands of the market and fulfil our population’s expectations for effective climate protection,” she said.

text:
Tyson Foods is staying quiet about the prospective sale of Washington’s largest beef packing plant.

With little information to go on Washington’s $5.8 billion beef industry is watching nervously and contemplating if beef cattle raised in the Northwest will be processed here or gets sent to packing plants in Idaho, Utah or beyond.

Tyson rocked the industry in August when it announced it was “pursuing” a deal to sell its plant at Wallula Gap, east of Pasco. No buyer has been identified.

Tyson, based in Springdale, Ark., did not respond to several requests for an update.

Entire industry watching

“I think the entire industry in the Pacific Northwest is watching this very closely because of the critical role that plant plays,” said Jack Fields, a cattle producer as well as executive director of the Washington Cattle Feeders Association.

His members are concentrated in Franklin, Yakima, Grant and Adams counties and rely on Tyson to process their cattle into beef.

The move comes as Tyson says it is focusing its business on facilities in Nebraska, Kansas and Texas, calling it a strategy to manage an ongoing cattle shortage.

The shift includes closing facilities in Illinois and Utah.

It has given no indication who might buy the plant or if it will continue to operate it if no buyer is found.

Fields said he’s heard no news about a possible buyer, but said it’s critical it keeps operating. Tyson processes domestic and Canadian-fed cattle, including his own.

Fields said he’s hoping for a buyer and a seamless transition.

“Our industry needs certainty. The last thing we need is uncertainty at the very end of the production chain,” he said.

If the Northwest loses some of its capacity to process cattle, they could be transported to another state, adding significant expense.

Major employer

Tyson isn’t just raising concerns in the state’s beef industry.

It is a significant employer in Walla Walla County, where the plant is located, and in the Tri-Cities, where many of its 1,400 workers live.

Tyson is the largest private employer in Walla Walla County and the fourth-largest private employer in the Tri-Cities, trailing Kadlec Regional Medical Center, Lamb Weston Holdings Inc. and First Fruits Farms, according to Tri-City Development Council (TRIDEC) figures.

Tyson Foods advertises wages of $22.35 an hour for a variety of processing jobs at its Wallula Gap plant, with actual wages varying based on shifts and other processing jobs, including meat cutting on its company hiring site.

By comparison, Amazon advertises jobs for warehouse equipment operators at $20.25-$21.75 an hour and Darigold advertises wet processing operator jobs at $27.19-$28.28 an hour.

But its impact also goes beyond the immediate neighborhood.

$5.85B beef industry

Tyson and its many partners and vendors anchor an industry worth $5.85 billion to the Washington economy, according to a 2024 economic impact report.

The report was commissioned by the Washington Beef Commission and completed by a Washington State University researcher.

The beef industry generated $3.12 billion through sales of finished cows and calf, feed yard operations and processing sectors. Indirect impacts added $2.71 billion to the total when vendors and other partners are factored in.

Washington’s cattle industry is highly local, using suppliers and services within the state. That translates to $4.35 for every $1 spent, the statement said.

Tyson Foods is its largest player.

Tyson was the nation’s second-leading beef processor in 2024, according to National Cattlemen’s Beef Association statistics. Tyson operated six plants at the time.

Its Wallula Gap/Pasco plant can process about 2,000 head per day, representing a significant percentage of beef cattle harvested in the state.

There were 88,000 cattle slaughtered in July, according to the most figures compiled by the USDA’s National Agricultural Statistics Service.

Boise-based Agri Beef Foods LLC operates Washington Beef, the state’s other major packing plant. The Toppenish plant has a reported processing capacity of 1,550 head per day.

The next significant facility is a JBS USA beef plant in Hyrum, Utah.

“Cull” cows, typically cattle culled from breeding and dairy herds, are processed in smaller facilities.

Neither Agri Beef nor JBS could be reached to comment on their potential interest in the plant.

Aviation fuel connection

The cattle industry has partners in unexpected places too.

SkyNRG, a sustainable aviation fuel company that turns waste into jet fuel, plans to establish a production facility next to Tyson Foods at Wallula Gap.

While it has said it will use cattle waste, a spokesman said its future is not tied to the plant. SkyNRG refers to its Wallula Gap plan as “Project Wigeon.” Its future is not tied to Tyson, it said in a statement to the Tri-City Herald.

“Even if the Tyson plant were to close, it would not impact Project Wigeon’s ability to produce SAF at our full capacity of 50 million gallons per year,” it told the Tri-City Herald.

text:
By DEREK TELLIER

Editor

Minnesota soybean farmers are heading toward harvest with strong crops in parts of McLeod County, but high production costs, drought elsewhere in the state, and uncertainty surrounding trade and biofuel policy continue to weigh on the industry.

Brownton farmer Ryan Mackenthun, president of the Minnesota Soybean Growers Association, recently had an opportunity to bring those concerns directly to state lawmakers during a meeting with Minnesota Sens. Nick Frentz and Aric Putnam at Minnesota Soybean headquarters in Mankato.

Mackenthun said the senators asked to meet with the organization, giving growers an opportunity to discuss current conditions for soybean producers and issues the organization expects farmers to face in the coming years.

“We are always excited to chat with our policymakers,” Mackenthun said, adding that the organization wants decisions affecting agriculture to be based on science and factual information.

Rising costs squeeze farmers

For Mackenthun, many of the pressures facing farmers begin with what it costs to put a crop in the ground.

He pointed to high equipment prices, interest rates, fertilizer costs, and diesel prices as challenges for producers. Global events can quickly make those pressures worse, he said, particularly when they affect energy and fertilizer supplies.

Protecting farmers’ access to crop inputs will remain a priority for the Minnesota Soybean Growers Association, according to Mackenthun.

Biofuels are another major focus. Mackenthun said the organization has been involved in disputes over policies it believes could affect demand for soybean-based fuels, including Minnesota’s vehicle emissions regulations and federal decisions involving small refinery exemptions under the Renewable Fuel Standard.

Mackenthun said increases in federal renewable fuel blending requirements have helped stimulate domestic demand for soybeans. He said he discussed the importance of those requirements with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins during Farmfest.

Looking beyond

traditional biodiesel

Mackenthun sees additional opportunities for soybean farmers as biodiesel use expands into industries beyond conventional highway transportation.

He pointed to rail companies considering higher biodiesel blends and maritime operators exploring biodiesel for ocean-going vessels. He also cited the City of Edina’s planned use of B100, or 100% biodiesel, in municipal utility vehicles.

The opportunity Mackenthun believes could have the largest effect, however, is sustainable aviation fuel.

Getting sustainable aviation fuel established in the aviation industry could create another significant market for agricultural feedstocks, he said. Mackenthun pointed to Europe’s use of aviation fuel blending requirements as an example of how that market could develop.

McLeod County crops

enter harvest in good shape

Closer to home, Mackenthun said McLeod County farmers have had reason for optimism heading into harvest.

“Our immediate area was one of the last to go into a drought category in the state,” he said.

Timely rains helped crops locally, and Mackenthun described fields in McLeod County as looking “fantastic.”

Conditions have not been as favorable everywhere. Mackenthun said farmers do not have to travel far north or southwest to find areas where drought has taken a heavier toll. He said crop insurance could become particularly important for producers struggling with reduced production.

Global events reach

Minnesota farms

Trade remains another piece of the financial picture, particularly for soybeans.

Mackenthun said China’s purchases remain closely watched because of the country’s importance to soybean exports. Based on information he had seen, Mackenthun said China was approaching half of its purchasing commitment for the marketing year as harvest approached, traditionally an important period for soybean purchases.

At the same time, he said international disruptions can reach Minnesota farms through the prices producers pay for necessities such as diesel and fertilizer.

Mackenthun pointed specifically to disruptions involving the Strait of Hormuz, saying they affect crude oil and urea fertilizer supplies and illustrate how events thousands of miles away can influence production costs in Minnesota.

Still, Mackenthun said stronger domestic use and improving exports could help reduce U.S. soybean and corn inventories.

For farmers dealing with high costs and uncertain markets, he said the hope is that tightening supplies and stronger demand will eventually shift the economics of growing row crops back toward profitability.

NEW YORK — Companies will need coordinated action from the government, suppliers and customers to meet sustainability goals, Delta Air Lines and Uber leaders said at Axios House at Climate Week and the UN General Assembly.

Why it matters: The push to make travel more sustainable is colliding with the costs of adaptation and lack of supporting infrastructure.

Axios' Alan Neuhauser moderated conversations with Delta Air Lines chief sustainability officer Amelia DeLuca and Uber global head of mobility sustainability Santosh Rao. The Sept. 22 event was sponsored by Hilton.

State of play: Delta recently reframed its 50% net-zero target by 2050 as an "aspiration" after previously describing it as an "ultimate goal." The company remains committed to its 10% sustainable aviation fuel target by 2030.

What they're saying: Partnerships are the core of a successful sustainable travel strategy.

Delta has a "multiyear, long-term strategic partnership with Shell," DeLuca said, and "they're helping us with the logistics and the infrastructure, the sourcing of that sustainable aviation fuel."

"There needs to be continued government support — federal, state and internationally," DeLuca added. "We are sure going to try" to meet the SAF threshold, "but it's really a team effort."

"This is going to be a team sport," Rao said. "We're not going to be able to do it alone."

Zoom in: Government subsidies will be necessary "for quite some time" to help sustainable aviation fuel compete with conventional jet fuel, DeLuca said.

What we're watching: A recent survey showed that charger access is the biggest barrier to electric vehicle adoption. To address this, Uber launched a pilot in France this week allowing drivers to find and pay for charging directly in the app, Rao said.

"We're looking forward to rolling that [out] to more markets globally," Rao said.

The Managing Director of the Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) H. Shankar on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) said the company was looking at how it could be a part of the growth journey in renewable energy. “CBG (compressed bio-gas) is fuel that can be a good form of energy we can invest in. With SAF (sustainable aviation fuel), we can be a part of sustainability in aviation fuel,” Mr. Shankar said at a fireside chat during the CPCL-The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 with The Hindu’s senior deputy editor N. Ravikumar.

This past August has been a very important milestone in the automobile sector, with more renewable, hybrid EV (electric vehicles) and CNG (compressed natural gas) vehicles registered than vehicles using hydrocarbon derivatives as fuel, Mr. Shankar said.

“We are watching the transition that is happening now. Although the impact is more on on two- and three-wheelers, it’s only a matter of time before it (renewable energy) really changes the larger means of transportation also. Refineries will continue to thrive despite the shift in automobiles from fossil-based fuels to renewable energy. We will change our refining from a fuel-based one to a petrochemical-based one, according to the needs of our customers,” Mr. Shankar said.

Speaking of CPCL’s refinery at Manali, Mr. Shankar said the company was building its own infrastructure requirements for importing green power directly, and had started using green energy in its day-to-day operations. “So, this is how we are preparing ourselves also for the transition from fossil fuel to renewable energy as a means of energy supply for processing requirements,” he said.

At Nagapattinam, where CPCL is in a joint venture with Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) and had originally proposed a nine-million tonnes per annum refinery, and a small component of polypropylene with petrochemical feedstock, the company is taking an alternative route. “Looking at the the internal rate of return that is accruing from the project, we are looking at the opportunity to move into the petrochemical sector directly,” Mr. Shankar said.

On the company being accorded ‘Navratna’ status, Mr. Shankar said it was a recognition from the Government of India, which came with a lot of benefits, and also a lot of responsibility and accountability. “Our board has now the authority to sanction the approval of projects without any limit on a standalone basis. We also have lot of flexibility with respect to the formation of joint ventures to move forward,” he said.

“Earlier our proposals for ₹500 crore and above would go to IOCL for further approvals. Now, the whole power rests with us. So, we have to do our own due diligence thoroughly because whatever we do now, it goes directly into the execution mode. And our accountability to stakeholders also increases manifold,” Mr. Shankar said, adding, “So, I would say this status comes with lot of responsibility, and we are we are ready for that.”

The summit is supported by Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) as the Presenting Partner, with NLC India Limited, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Navin’s, WABAG, Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited, Indian Bank, Urbando and State Bank of India as Associate Partners.

The summit’s sustainability-focused partnerships include Thermax as the Sustainable Cooling Partner, Treeni as the Sustainability Intelligence Partner, Chennai Port Authority as the Blue Economy Partner and Tamil Nadu Green Climate Company as the Climate Action Partner.

title: Remarks by Senior Minister of State for Transport Mr Murali Pillai at the Passenger Terminal ...
description:
Good morning, and a warm welcome to the inaugural Passenger Terminal Expo Asia.

As Asian economies became more connected and integrated with the world, airports such as Changi, Chek Lap Kok and Incheon became powerful portals for tourism, trade and investment.
That international framework still underpins civil aviation today.
Singapore is honoured to host the inaugural Passenger Terminal Expo Asia and be a part of these conversations.
text:
The Power of Connections: Aviation in Asia

Mr Aloysius Arlando, Chairman of Asia for CloserStill Media

Mr Sopon Piyapanee, Assistant Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Transport, Thailand

Mr Peter Massey, Commercial Director for CloserStill Media

Mr Jayson Goh, Executive Vice President for Airport Management at Changi Airport Group

Excellencies and distinguished guests

Introduction

1. Good morning, and a warm welcome to the inaugural Passenger Terminal Expo Asia. It is a pleasure to join so many leaders from across the global aviation community here in Singapore.

2. We are gathered to talk about airport terminals, systems, and technology. But at its heart, our industry is not just about infrastructure – what we do, is the business of connecting people.

Lessons from the Past

3. Asia's aviation story began earlier than many assume, and began modestly.

a. Don Mueang opened in 1914, with commercial flights following a decade later. It remains one of the oldest continuously operating airports in the world, and still serves Bangkok today.

b. In 1929, the British built a wooden aerodrome at Taiping, in Perak, one of the first airfields in Malaya. Among its earliest regular services was a flight that brought in the day's newspapers for the town.

c. Singapore's first purpose-built civilian airport opened at Kallang in 1937, on a reclaimed mangrove swamp, with a circular grass landing field designed to take both land planes and seaplanes. Eight days after it opened, Amelia Earhart landed there on her attempt to fly around the world. She described it as an aviation miracle of the East.

d. And in 1940, Kemayoran opened in Jakarta as the first purpose-built international airport in the region's largest archipelago, linking its cities to Southeast Asia and to Australia.

4. By today's standards, these were small airports. Grass strips, a few flights a week, and a handful of passengers. But each represented the hunger for human connection – each of our countries did not stand alone, and we laboured to be connected with the rest of the world.

5. As traffic grew, Governments had to choose between taking many small steps or one big one. Singapore chose one big step for man. In 1975, we decided to relocate our airport from Paya Lebar to Changi. It was a massive undertaking that required extensive reclamation, new infrastructure and the overnight transfer of airport operations. But Singapore’s future depended on connectivity.

6. Elsewhere in Asia, big steps were also taken.

a. Many in this room will remember Hong Kong’s Kai Tak Airport and its iconic checkerboard approach over Kowloon, where pilots made a dramatic turn towards the runway above the densely built-up city. But it became clear that Hong Kong needed a larger airport to support its future development, leading to the move to Chek Lap Kok.

b. Korea made a similarly bold bet with Incheon, shifting operations from the older Gimpo Airport in 2001 to provide capacity for future growth.

c. We witnessed this in China and in India too. Beijing Capital Airport's Terminal 3, opened ahead of the 2008 Olympics, and Delhi's Terminal 3, opened before the 2010 Commonwealth Games, reflecting the growing confidence and international ambitions of these two economies becoming increasingly connected to the world.

7. The lesson is clear. Airports are not just built for the traffic of their day, but for the growth still to come.

8. These decisions transformed their cities and the lives of their people. As Asian economies became more connected and integrated with the world, airports such as Changi, Chek Lap Kok and Incheon became powerful portals for tourism, trade and investment.

9. Looking back, these decision look obvious. But in reality, they demanded vision, sustained investment, and the conviction that connectivity would create a new world that did not exist then.

Investing for the Long-Term

10. That conviction is needed again. ICAO expects global passenger numbers to nearly triple by 2050, with Asia-Pacific accounting for a significant share. Across the region, airports are expanding, routes are launching, and governments are investing heavily.

11. But our challenge is not the same as those of the old. For them, the central question was capacity. For us, it is not just one question but many – we must grow while contending with tighter labour markets, rising passenger expectations, greater operational uncertainty, and a shrinking carbon envelope.

12. In this, the airport experience is key.

a. For airlines, airport experience is a commercial consideration: it shapes turnaround times, reliability, and the cost of doing business.

b. For passengers, the experience includes how they move through our terminals, whether they catch their connection or arrive at a meeting on time. The airport experience can also shape their impression of the city.

13. In Singapore, the question we ask ourselves is: how do we ensure that Changi remains a trusted hub of choice for airlines and passengers alike?

What Singapore is Doing

14. Much of what we have done, we learnt from others in this room. Let me share where we are placing our bets going ahead.

15. First, we invest ahead of demand. Changi has grown from a single terminal in the 1980s into a four-terminal air hub with direct links to more than 170 cities today. When Terminal 5 is ready in the mid-2030s, it will add capacity for 50 million passengers per annum, supporting our ambition to connect to more than 200 cities.

16. But increasing capacity is only one part of the story. We are also testing new technologies, services and operating concepts to make travel more seamless while enabling the airport to operate more efficiently.

a. Self-service check-in and bag drop are now ubiquitous. Eligible travellers clear immigration using facial and iris biometrics, without needing to present a passport.

b. Our attention has turned to baggage, which many travellers still regard as a source of inconvenience. Our aim is not simply to move bags more efficiently, but to reduce friction in the travel journey. Building on similar initiatives by airports such as Hong Kong and Incheon, we are trialling Off-Airport Check-In. By leveraging Singapore’s hotel ecosystem, eligible travellers can check-in and leave their luggage at participating hotels for transfer to their flight, bringing airport services closer to where travellers already are. Travellers can then enjoy their final day in Singapore, baggage-free, and hopefully more time for shopping as well.

c. We are also deploying autonomous wheelchairs, which give passengers with reduced mobility greater independence, while allowing our staff to focus on those who need more assistance

d. These initiatives will be trialled before being incorporated into Terminal 5.

Building a Sustainable Future

17. Of the many challenges facing our generation, sustainability may be the most consequential.

18. Demand for air travel will keep on growing. The question is whether it can grow in a way that is both economically and environmentally sustainable.

19. Solutions already exist. Sustainable Aviation Fuel, or SAF, and electric airside vehicles are available today. However, cost remains a critical barrier. SAF remains two to five times more expensive than conventional jet fuel. Electric airside vehicles, where available, likewise come with a price premium and require costly grid infrastructure to support them.

20. But standing still is not an option. Decarbonisation projects often require significant investment before their technologies mature and their commercial benefits are fully realised. Waiting for uncertainties to disappear would cost us valuable time.

21. So, a key enabler is green aviation financing, which encouragingly, is already taking shape in Asia.

a. In Pakistan, the Asian Development Bank and International Finance Corporation are supporting a new SAF facility through blended financing and a long-term offtake agreement with Shell.

b. Airport operators are also tapping capital markets. Airport Authority Hong Kong issued a US$1 billion green bond tranche in 2023 to finance green projects under its Sustainable Finance Framework.

c. These examples show that sustainable aviation is not just an environmental imperative. It is increasingly an infrastructure and investment opportunity.

The Power of Collaboration

22. We are in the business of connections, and so we must all realise that none of this can be done by any single airport, airline or government. Bringing viable solutions to scale requires a coalition of willing partners. Governments can provide policy certainty. Airports and airlines can create demand and develop viable projects. Technology providers can keep on innovating. And financiers can mobilise capital, allocate risk and help bring promising solutions to scale.

23. Our industry is born into connections. Global aviation grew because countries came together, agreed to abide by common rules, collective standards, and shared principles. The 1944 Chicago Convention laid the foundations for ICAO. That international framework still underpins civil aviation today. As Asia grows in the decades ahead, multilateralism must matter more, not less.

Why This Expo Matters

24. Passenger Terminal Expo has long been the premier global platform for exchanging ideas and shaping the future of our industry. This year, for the first time, that conversation comes to Asia.

25. This is fitting. The region that will generate the largest share of aviation's growth should not simply adopt solutions developed elsewhere. It should help shape them.

26. In this hall are the people who actually design, build, finance and run airports. Much of what will become standard practice in the 2030s is sitting on this show floor today as a prototype.

Conclusion

27. Let me conclude.

28. I have spoken about how the airports that transformed Asia were built for the growth that was still to come. Our responsibility is to show the same foresight today. The conversations we have, the partnerships we form, and the investments we make will help shape how millions of people travel in the decades ahead.

29. Singapore is honoured to host the inaugural Passenger Terminal Expo Asia and be a part of these conversations.

30. The next two days is a meeting of minds – of all of us, who, saw and believed in the transformative power of aviation, and of determination, cooperation and long-term commitment.

31. Aviation transformed Asia of the past, and from this history, we will shape the transformation of our future. Thank you.

text:
NEW YORK — With 2.5% profit margins and the harsh reality of aviation physics, Alaska Air Group needs to be strategic when betting on low-carbon technology. That includes partnering with Bill Gates’ Breakthrough Energy Ventures on sustainable aviation fuel and backing companies developing fuel-efficient aircraft.

Those were two takeaways from Ryan Spies, Alaska Air’s managing director of sustainability, speaking Wednesday at Bloomberg Green New York.

Aviation contributes 2.5% of global carbon dioxide emissions, but can account for up to 5% of global warming due to additional atmospheric effects, experts say.

Currently, the primary strategy for curbing emissions is using sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. Made from sources such as used cooking oil, agricultural waste, forestry waste and captured carbon, SAF can be blended with conventional jet fuel. The trouble is that production comes nowhere near matching demand, supplying less than 1% of aviation fuel today.

To address the shortage, Seattle-based Alaska Air Group — parent company of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines — partnered last year with other carriers and Breakthrough to create a $150 million fund backing SAF innovators. The fund relies on Breakthrough’s experts to identify the most viable feedstocks, smartest chemistries, and strongest economics.

And while SAF has typically been much more expensive than conventional fuels, the Iran War and its impacts on international oil shipping is changing that math.

“Six months ago, sustainable aviation fuel was absolutely more expensive than jet fuel,” Spies said at the event, which is part of Climate Week NYC. “If you went to a producer of SAF today, you can get a pretty competitive price compared to jet.”

The market volatility has also heightened interest in SAF as a tool for U.S. energy independence, rather than just an environmentally friendly alternative.

In January, Pacific Northwest officials from organizations including Alaska Air, Amazon, Boeing, SkyNRG and government representatives launched the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator to establish the region as a SAF hub. Startup Twelve is already producing fuel in Moses Lake, Wash., and Montana Renewables has emerged as a sector leader.

While SAF is being deployed today, Alaska Air is also eyeing next-generation aircraft designs. Two years ago, the airline announced an investment in JetZero, a company developing a blended-wing body aircraft that aims to slash fuel use in half. JetZero hopes to fly a prototype next year and begin carrying passengers in 2030, the Seattle Times reported Sunday.

“An aircraft that can carry “200 plus passengers that can reduce fuel usage by 50% through better aerodynamics — that’s a game-changing development,” Spies said.

Alaska Air has also backed Ampaire, a startup Spies called “the Prius of aviation” due to its hybrid-electric drivetrain. The system is currently designed for smaller, eight-seat aircraft, and Spies said the company was excited to bring Ampaire to Hawaii.

Although a blended-wing aircraft would be a noticeable departure from today’s flying experience, climate-related changes coming to the aviation over the next decade will be less obvious as the fuel changes and incremental advances are made.

Advancing aviation sustainability remains a slow process and one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize, Spies said, “because of pure physics.”

title: AVIATION EXCEEDS THE SUSTAINABLE FUEL THRESHOLD, BUT NOT THE SUPPLY ...
description:
The first annual ReFuelEU Aviation report, published on 17 September by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, puts the share of sustainable aviation fuels supplied at EU airports in 2025 at 2.8%.
Of the 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel supplied, 1.1 million tonnes fell into this category.
Supply increased from 193,000 tonnes in 2024 to 1.1 million tonnes in 2025.
EASA estimates that the substitution of conventional fuel avoided 3.77 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025.
The expected action is to compare actual purchases with regulatory trajectories, diversify feedstocks and examine compliance supplier by supplier.
text:
The first annual ReFuelEU Aviation report, published on 17 September by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, puts the share of sustainable aviation fuels supplied at EU airports in 2025 at 2.8%. Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 required a minimum share of 2% for that year. Of the 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel supplied, 1.1 million tonnes fell into this category. This is an aggregate market measure, not a certificate showing that every supplier individually complied with its obligation.

Supply increased from 193,000 tonnes in 2024 to 1.1 million tonnes in 2025. Sustainable fuels were supplied at 121 airports across the 27 Member States, representing 79% of EU airports, compared with 33 airports the previous year.

EASA estimates that the substitution of conventional fuel avoided 3.77 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025. This is an agency calculation that depends on the characteristics of the fuels and the methodology used, not a direct measurement of all emissions from the aviation sector. Operators and airports therefore need to assess the data against the volumes actually available at their own supply points.

The European Union produces 86% of the sustainable fuels consumed at these airports, but the feedstocks used to produce 85% of those volumes originate outside the Union. Used cooking oil still accounts for 80% of the total.

Production and supply therefore do not tell the same story of industrial sovereignty. Five countries, the Netherlands, Spain, Germany, Italy and France, account for 74% of the observed supply. This geography affects transport, competition for feedstocks and the ability of smaller airports to secure long-term contracts.

Fuel availability alone does not determine how supply is distributed. A supplier concentrated at a major airport faces a different constraint from an operator serving peripheral airports. Contracts, storage capacity and reporting rules determine the reliability of the local picture.

The report makes it possible to examine these issues without attributing an infringement to any operator on the basis of a European average. It also highlights the need to establish the origin of used oils and the robustness of certification chains as demand increases.

EASA considers projected production capacity compatible with the overall 6% blending target for 2030. Synthetic fuel, however, remains at an early stage. One demonstration plant exists in the Union, while around fifty projects are awaiting a final investment decision.

Projected capacity does not deliver a single litre until financing, electricity, feedstocks and offtake contracts have been secured. The report does not create a new obligation, but it makes the first year of an already applicable mandate verifiable. The expected action is to compare actual purchases with regulatory trajectories, diversify feedstocks and examine compliance supplier by supplier.

text:
Uniper Inks Landmark Agreement for Synthetic Green Jet Fuels with Arcadia eFuels

Major Deal Signals Progress in Sustainable Aviation Fuel Adoption

Uniper and Arcadia eFuels Sign Long-Term eSAF Agreement

FRANKFURT, Sept 23 (Reuters) - German state-owned utility Uniper signed a deal to procure synthetic sustainable jet fuel (eSAF) from US-based Arcadia eFuels, the companies said on Wednesday.

Uniper will buy 40,000 metric tons of the fuel annually for more than 10 years, supplied by Arcadia eFuels' Endor project in Denmark, under the agreement, which the companies in a statement said was one of the largest eSAF offtake agreements to date.

The Challenge of Decarbonising Aviation

Aviation is among the toughest industries to decarbonise, leaving green fuels with lower emissions than conventional jet fuel as one of the few options to cut air travel pollution.

Scaling Up Sustainable Aviation Fuels

"The key challenge now is to move sustainable aviation fuels from promising projects to industrial scale," said Uniper CEO Michael Lewis. "For Uniper, it is also an important step in building a strong position in a market with significant growth potential," he added.

Impact and Future Supply Projections

Supplies are expected from the early 2030s and would cover the fuel equivalent of around 1,000 Boeing 787-9 flights from Duesseldorf in Germany, where Uniper is based, to Abu Dhabi each year, the companies said.

Industry Perspectives on eSAF

"eSAF is not only a fuel of the future – it is a present-day answer to the aviation sector's demand for diversification of supply, and today's agreement brings that solution meaningfully closer to expanding production within the EU," Arcadia eFuels CEO Amy Hebert said.

Regulatory Landscape for Sustainable Aviation Fuels in the EU

Upcoming EU Mandates

The EU required 2% of fuel made available at regional airports to be SAF in ​2025, rising to ⁠6% in 2030, while eSAF must account for 1.2% of the total from 2030, rising to 5% in 2035.

text:
Infinium on Sept. 21 introduced its mSAF product offering, a new methane-derived sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) platform which converts renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas, and other qualified methane streams into low-carbon aviation fuel. The new offering expands the feedstocks and locations available for Infinium projects while complementing the company's growing CO₂-based eSAF business.

The expansion addresses a fundamental challenge for aviation: no single feedstock pathway can produce all of the low-carbon fuel needed to satisfy rising SAF mandates and industry commitments. Renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas and other methane streams are already aggregated at landfills, dairies, wastewater facilities and gas-gathering systems across North America, Asia, Europe and other geographies and are increasingly looking for diversified end use opportunities.

"mSAF expands what Infinium's platform can do. It gives us another way to apply our proven technology, develop projects across a broader range of locations and deliver more low-carbon fuel alongside our growing eSAF business. Aviation needs multiple scalable pathways, and Infinium is positioned to continue to deliver options,” said Robert Schuetzle, CEO, Infinium

One proven technology, two feedstock pathways

Infinium has more than a decade of experience converting gases into liquid hydrocarbons with its synthesis technology deployed across commercial installations. Synthesize™ — Infinium's proprietary advanced Fischer–Tropsch catalyst and reactor design for converting syngas into liquid hydrocarbons — is also used to produce Infinium eFuels today. The two product lines share core synthesis technology, catalyst manufacturing, product specifications and certification pathways.

Electrified reforming improves yield and carbon performance

Infinium's mSAF platform also utilizes its proprietary Reform™ package - a proprietary electric steam methane reformer (eSMR) designed to produce syngas with a lower carbon footprint than a traditional gas-fired SMR. Infinium is deploying the world's largest eSMR at Project Roadrunner, for conversion of methane into syngas.

Conventional steam methane reforming burns a portion of the feed gas to produce process heat. This adds combustion emissions to the fuel's lifecycle footprint and consumes feedstock carbon that could otherwise be converted into the finished product.

Infinium's Reform technology uses renewable electricity to provide that process heat. This keeps more feedstock carbon available for conversion, increasing fuel yield per unit of gas, while avoiding the reforming-related combustion emissions associated with conventional systems. For RNG projects, where feedstock cost and carbon intensity are central to commercial performance, greater yield and lower reforming emissions directly improve project economics.

text:
London, United Kingdom | 22–23 September 2026

Alkagesta participated in the SAF Global Summit 2026 in London — one of the most significant gatherings in the sustainable aviation fuel industry, bringing together over 1,000 senior executives from across the SAF value chain, including policymakers, energy leaders, producers, investors, airlines, and OEMs. The summit’s 2026 edition was built around four key pillars: robust policy, strategic investment, scaled production and supply chain logistics, and innovative technologies.

Alkagesta was represented by Alex Yusifli, Business Development Manager, and Alasgar Guliyev, Operations Manager, who engaged with industry participants across the two-day programme.

Key themes addressed during the summit that are directly relevant to Alkagesta’s operations included:

The regulatory roadmap to commercial-scale SAF — including the UK SAF Mandate, ReFuelEU, and the US Inflation Reduction Act as frameworks driving investment certainty

How leading suppliers and producers are addressing the 2030 SAF supply gap, including feedstock diversification, project financing, and offtake momentum from airlines and corporate buyers

SAF pricing dynamics in Europe — supply constraints, demand signals, and the commercial implications for traders and distributors

Feedstock frontiers — scaling sustainable supply through diversified non-food sources, efficient collection logistics, and advanced preprocessing infrastructure

Building global SAF corridors connecting production centres to supply hubs, including the expansion of book-and-claim systems for transparency and traceability in SAF transactions

The European refining sector’s role as the industrial backbone of SAF production, and the pathway from renewable feedstocks to commercial-scale output

Alkagesta holds ISCC and CORSIA certification, enabling the company to trade and supply CORSIA-eligible sustainable aviation fuel across multiple sustainability jurisdictions. The company also recently gained access to EU ETS allowances, complementing its SAF and biofuels trading capabilities and positioning Alkagesta to support clients across a broader set of carbon compliance obligations. Earlier in 2026, Alkagesta secured access to the NATO Central Europe Pipeline System (CEPS), enabling the delivery of jet fuel blended with sustainable aviation fuel directly to airlines — a development that reflects both the company’s growing presence in the aviation fuels market and the rigorous compliance standards it meets as a trusted supply chain partner.

For Alkagesta, participation in the SAF Global Summit 2026 reinforced the growing commercial importance of sustainable aviation fuel as a core component of the company’s biofuels and sustainable fuels strategy, as demand for certified SAF continues to grow across European and global aviation markets.

text:
HOUSTON, TX / ACCESS Newswire / September 23, 2026 / ABGi USA has added carbon capture and clean fuel production tax credit services to its growing portfolio of energy incentives, extending support to businesses undertaking a wider range of energy and decarbonization projects.

The additions include the Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit, Section 45Q, and the Clean Fuel Production Credit, Section 45Z. Together with ABGi USA's existing capabilities in clean energy investment, advanced manufacturing, and clean hydrogen incentives, the expanded portfolio allows the firm to support projects across multiple stages of the energy transition.

Section 45Q provides performance-based tax credits for qualifying facilities that capture and store carbon oxides rather than releasing them into the atmosphere. Depending on applicable requirements, qualifying projects may generate credits for up to 12 years after a facility is placed in service.

Section 45Z supports qualifying production of low-carbon fuels, including biofuels and sustainable aviation fuel, with potential credit value tied to verified lifecycle emissions.

These additions build on ABGi USA's broader energy incentive capabilities, which also include investment tax credits for qualifying clean energy technologies under Sections 48 and 48E, production-based incentives for qualifying domestic manufacturers under Section 45X, and credits for low-emission hydrogen production under Section 45V.

The value of these incentives can vary significantly depending on the type of project. Some may help reduce the effective cost of a capital investment, while others are tied to production, emissions performance, or qualifying activity over multiple years.

For businesses evaluating new facilities, energy infrastructure, manufacturing expansion, carbon reduction initiatives, hydrogen production, or cleaner fuel technologies, understanding which incentives may apply can help provide a more complete view of project economics and potential value.

"As energy projects become increasingly complex, businesses need to understand how federal incentives can support their investments. Expanding into carbon capture and clean fuel incentives allows us to help clients identify more opportunities and maximize the value of projects they are already pursuing," said Kris Huffman, Associate Director, Strategic Incentives & Capital Solutions.

ABGi USA's specialized energy incentive experts help organizations evaluate potential eligibility, estimate credit value, and navigate the technical and compliance requirements associated with qualifying projects.

Businesses with questions about a current or planned project can connect with ABGi USA to better understand which energy incentives may apply and how those opportunities could support broader investment goals.

text:
Deepak Maheshwari, CEO, Essar Energy Transition Fuels, shares insights on Stanlow’s investment programme with Business Today

Essar is advancing a £4.3 billion investment pipeline through 2035 to transform its Stanlow refinery in the UK into a major energy transition hub, with more than £1 billion of projects nearing Final Investment Decision (FID), Deepak Maheshwari, CEO, Essar Energy Transition Fuels, told Business Today.

Maheshwari said the investment programme will be deployed in phases, with low-carbon hydrogen production and low-carbon heat expected to progress first, followed by larger-scale sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other growth projects in the early 2030s.

According to Maheshwari, the strategy is aimed at transforming Stanlow into what Essar describes as the world’s first low-carbon process refinery, with an objective of reducing emissions by up to 95% by the 2030s. The plan centres on low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, electrification, low-carbon heat and power, and efficiency improvements.

“Hydrogen is central to Essar’s energy transition strategy,” Maheshwari said. The company is developing a 350MW low-carbon hydrogen plant, involving an investment of around £1.5 billion, as part of the HyNet North West industrial decarbonisation cluster.

Maheshwari said the next phase will include sustainable aviation fuel. Essar is developing a Methanol-to-Jet project targeting production of around 200,000 tonnes of advanced SAF annually in the early 2030s. The company is also developing SAF in India for the UK market.

Essar has already invested around £1 billion in modernising and upgrading Stanlow since acquiring the refinery from Shell in 2011. Maheshwari said these investments included a move to single-train operation, a catalytic cracker upgrade, a £100 million turnaround that increased throughput by around 8%, and investment in the UK’s first hydrogen-ready refinery furnace.

Maheshwari said Stanlow has capacity to meet around 25% of the UK’s refining requirements and supplies around 20% of the country’s transport fuels and 12.5% of total UK jet fuel demand.

On funding, Maheshwari said the £4.3 billion programme will be financed through a combination of Essar equity, project-level financing and government-supported mechanisms. He said the company does not disclose the precise funding mix, while government support is particularly important for low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture and advanced SAF projects.

The investment also has an India-UK dimension. Maheshwari said the India-UK CETA could strengthen trade, investment and knowledge exchange between the two countries. He added that Essar could draw on specialist technology and expertise from its global operations, including India, for the Stanlow transformation.

Essar acquired Stanlow from Shell for $350 million in 2011. Maheshwari said the company brought operational, technical and engineering expertise from India, including experience from its 20 MTPA Vadinar refinery in Gujarat, to improve Stanlow’s efficiency and operational performance.

Maheshwari said Essar has already reduced emissions at Stanlow by 22% since acquiring the refinery in 2011. Fuel switching to low-carbon hydrogen and low-carbon heat and power is expected to deliver an initial reduction of about 30% of emissions, with carbon capture, electrification and efficiency improvements contributing to the longer-term 95% target.

On HyNet, Maheshwari said it is “absolutely central” to the decarbonisation strategy, providing the hydrogen and CO₂ transport and storage infrastructure required for Stanlow’s transformation.

He also identified policy and regulatory uncertainty as key risks to the investment programme, particularly decisions around hydrogen revenue support, carbon storage capacity and carbon-cost disparities with overseas competitors.

On the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, Maheshwari declined to comment on day-to-day commercial trading positions or refining margins. He said recent geopolitical events highlight the importance of resilient domestic refining capacity and diversified supply chains for UK energy security.

Maheshwari also said Essar is expanding its retail presence across the UK, with an ambition to reach up to 800 forecourts, representing around 9% of the UK market. Recently, Essar acquired 100% of SGN Retail for £400 million, adding 118 forecourts to its existing 117 sites. The combined network now has 235 forecourts, making Essar the eighth-largest forecourt network in the UK, with annual throughput of more than 650 million litres, Maheshwari said.

text:
Velocys has released the new AlphaCore™ 800 reactor, its highest-capacity microchannel Fischer-Tropsch (FT) reactor to date.

It is designed to produce up to 800 barrels per day, or 30,000 tonnes per year (30 kt/a) of FT fluids from a single reactor.

AlphaCore 800 doubles the capacity of AlphaCore 400 and extends Velocys' throughput-based AlphaCore reactor family from approximately 50 to 800 barrels per day per reactor (from 2 to 30 kt/a per reactor).

AlphaCore 800 is designed particularly for larger sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and e-fuels projects, including SAF plants targeting approximately 100,000 tonnes per year and above.

Benefits from expanding reactor size while preserving the underlying chemistry and design are clear: more FT capacity per reactor, enabling fewer reactors as project scale increases without sacrificing performance or reliability.

Reducing reactor count can simplify the FT island, reduce associated equipment requirements and lower FT unit cost.

For example, an FT plant requiring approximately 1,600 barrels per day (60 kt/a) of FT liquids could be configured with two AlphaCore 800 reactors.

This reduces total reactor count by 75% compared to an FT unit utilizing eight AlphaCore 200 reactors while maintaining the same FT liquids capacity.

"Customers are asking us to bring our microchannel FT technology into larger projects with simpler configurations," said Matthew Viergutz, CEO of Velocys.

"AlphaCore 800 is a direct response. As SAF projects move toward 100,000 tonnes per year and beyond, we are increasing capacity per reactor so developers can configure larger FT plants with fewer units while building on the technology platform and operating experience of Velocys."

AlphaCore 800 joins AlphaCore 50, 200 and 400 in the Velocys reactor portfolio, giving project developers a throughput-based product range built with the same core technology that can be applied across multiple project scales and syngas pathways.

text:
According to Gadkari, making better use of sugarcane by-products could also improve returns for farmers. (Image for representative purpose only)

India imports most of the fuel it consumes - be it crude oil, LPG, or even LNG. Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari has said that India’s agriculture sector can help drive down imported costs of fossil fuels, while at the same time using a combination of futuristic technology and a forward-looking vision if it is to become economically sustainable and help drive prosperity in rural India. Addressing the National Efficiency Awards ceremony organised by the National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories, Gadkari recently said producing sugar alone is no longer economically sustainable in view of global market conditions and the higher cost of production in India.

Make gas, ethanol, aviation fuel

Gadkari has called on sugar mills to expand into value-added by-products, particularly compressed bio-gas (CBG), ethanol, bio-manure and sustainable aviation fuel. "Instead of dumping waste into road embankments, if we convert it into gas - into CBG - our imports will decline. Understand this figure: Rs 22 lakh crore. We are sending Rs 22 lakh crore out of our country to import fossil fuels - petrol, diesel, and gas," Gadkari said according to ANI. He pointed out that India's sugar output is between 300 and 350 lakh tonnes, while domestic consumption ranges from 280 to 300 lakh tonnes. The resulting surplus has put pressure on sugar prices. At the same time, he said, countries such as Brazil have a significantly lower production cost, at Rs 23 per kg compared with India's Rs 33 to Rs 34 per kg. "The future of plain sugar is mediocre at best. I won't mince words: diversifying into complementary by-products guarantees a strong future," the Minister said. According to Gadkari, making better use of sugarcane by-products could also improve returns for farmers. He said the additional value generated through these products could eventually enable sugar mills to pay farmers as much as Rs 6,000 per tonne of sugarcane, compared with the current Rs 4,000. Gadkari also underlined the scale of India's agricultural waste and its potential as a source of bio-energy. Punjab and Haryana alone generate around 220 lakh tonnes of paddy stubble, he said. Five tonnes of stubble can produce one tonne of CBG, which he described as a way to address stubble burning and air pollution while simultaneously creating wealth in rural areas. "Technology has arrived, allowing us to produce CBG from stubble, bamboo, rice straw, bagasse, and Napier grass. The Government of India launched a dedicated scheme. Look at the numbers: 1,908 CBG plants have been registered across the country, with 132 already operational," he said. India has the potential to produce 50,000 tonnes of CBG per day, Gadkari said, but present output accounts for only around two per cent of that capacity. The government has also introduced mandatory procurement obligations along with a fixed procurement price of Rs 106 per kg. He said the initiative could bring Rs 2.5 lakh crore into the rural economy and create as many as 15 lakh jobs. The Minister further called on the sugar industry to make greater use of artificial intelligence, precision farming and agricultural drones to reduce the cost of inputs and improve farm productivity. He cited the decision to permit ethanol production directly from corn as an example, saying the move had resulted in Rs 45,000 crore being transferred directly to farmers in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

Barrier free tolling to save fuel and costs

Meanwhile, India is moving to a FASTag-enabled barrier-free tolling system which will not only save time, but also fuel costs. The government could gain an annual benefit of as much as Rs 25,000 crore once the electronic toll collection system FASTag is fully implemented, Gadkari said recently. Gadkari said the government is targeting the removal of barriers from all toll plazas on national highways by March 2027 as part of its plan to make toll collection completely barrier-free. "When the system will go fully live, then our department alone would deliver a benefit of Rs 20,000-25,000 crore per year to the Government of India because of the use of FASTags," Gadkari said at the Global Fintech Fest. The minister said FASTag adoption has already resulted in a 10% increase in toll collections, translating into an additional Rs 7,000 crore approximately. Total revenue generated at toll booths has consequently risen to more than Rs 82,000 crore, according to Gadkari.

text:
Insight Focus

US ethanol gains support from policy and export growth. The US Senate is moving closer to approving year-round E15 sales, supporting demand for corn and biofuels. Record ethanol exports prompted a bullish USDA outlook, while the EIA raised its 2027 production forecast. Iowa E15 sales reached their second-highest level on record and are on track to overtake E10 in 2026.

US Farm Bill Moves Closer to Authorising Year-Round E15

The US Senate Agriculture Committee on September 16 voted to advance the Agriculture Act of 2026, which includes provisions allowing year-round sales of E15 and support for the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry.

The action was applauded by all major farm and biofuel organisations. Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) President and CEO Geoff Cooper said, “There is broad bipartisan support for making lower-cost E15 available to consumers all year long, especially at a time when pump prices are on the rise and fuel supplies are tightening.”

The RFA urged the full Senate to pass year-round E15 legislation as quickly as possible, reconcile the language with the House version of the bill, and get a viable solution to President Trump’s desk for his signature.

Advocates of the Senate’s farm bill say it will provide farmers with a reliable market for corn and help lower fuel costs for consumers. Regular unleaded gasoline prices in the US averaged USD 4.475 on September 22, compared with USD 3.1843 a year ago and a high of USD 5.0165 on June 11, 2022, according to AAA data.

Source: AAA

The current extension of the 2018 Farm Bill is set to expire on September 30, 2026, roughly a month before the US midterm election. Previously, the Environmental Protection Agency allowed E15 sales during the summer through emergency waivers.

USDA Outlook Signals Continued Growth in Ethanol Exports

On the same day that the Senate advanced the farm bill out of committee, the USDA released the American Biofuels Trade Outlook, which was bullish on ethanol. The Outlook contains a plan that builds upon 2025’s record US ethanol export performance, removes restrictions on US biofuels, and secures new market opportunities for US farmers.

US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said that 2025 marked the strongest year for ethanol exports in US history. “The record-setting 2.2 billion gallons of US ethanol shipped around the world this past year, representing USD 4.7 billion, was not by accident,” the Secretary said.

Source: US Census Bureau Trade Data

“It represented the hard work of America’s farmers and demonstrates how American innovation and rural investment can deliver prosperity for consumers and producers at home and around the globe. American farmers are fuelling the future, and the American Biofuel Trade Outlook outlines the USDA’s plan to ensure that success continues, and America’s producers continue to prosper.”

Rising Export Demand Underpins Higher US Ethanol Output

On September 9, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) increased its forecast for 2027 fuel ethanol production in its latest Short-Term Energy Outlook. The outlook for 2027 fuel ethanol exports was also revised higher. The EIA maintained its forecast that fuel ethanol production will average 1.1 million barrels per day in 2026.

Production is currently expected to expand to 1.12 million barrels per day in 2027, up from the August outlook of 1.11 million barrels per day. Fuel ethanol production averaged 1.08 million barrels per day last year.

On a quarterly basis, fuel ethanol production is expected to average 1.09 million barrels per day during the third quarter of this year, increasing to 1.12 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter. Moving into 2027, fuel ethanol production is expected to average 1.11 million barrels per day during the first quarter, 1.1 million barrels per day during the second quarter, 1.12 million barrels per day during the third quarter, and 1.15 million barrels per day during the fourth quarter.

Source: EIA

According to a new report from the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), record ethanol exports in 2024 and 2025 were fuelled by growing global ethanol import demand and reduced competition from Brazil. Major ethanol-importing markets, including Canada, the EU, the UK, India, Colombia and the Philippines, increased their ethanol consumption, driving global import demand higher.

Source: US Census Bureau Trade Data

At the same time, strong domestic fuel ethanol demand in Brazil reduced exportable supplies and raised domestic prices, allowing the US to increase its share of a growing export market.

Iowa E15 Sales Approach Record Levels

Iowa fuel terminals distributed more than 46 million gallons of E15 during August, the second-highest amount on record, according to monthly fuel tax data released by the Iowa Department of Revenue.

title: Green Fuel Forward expands industry alliance to support SAF adoption in Asia
description:

Pedro Gomez, head, industry agenda, member of the executive committee, World Economic Forum, said, "With GenZero and dozens of private sector companies, we launched Green Fuel Forward to spark interest in SAF in the Asia-Pacific region.
text:
Green Fuel Forward, launched by GenZero and the World Economic Forum in May 2025 to scale demand for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), on Sept. 22 announced an expanded partnership structure and new members as it enters its next phase of market activation.

Announced during Green Markets Day at New York Climate Week, the expansion marks GFF's shift from building market awareness and procurement readiness to facilitating greater corporate action and participation in SAF and SAF certificates (SAFc) transactions across Asia.

GFF welcomed the Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) and the Singapore Sustainable Aviation Fuel Company (SAFCo) to its Steering Committee (SteerCo), alongside founding SteerCo member GenZero. The expanded SteerCo combines investment, demand-aggregation, procurement and market-development expertise as GFF works to translate growing corporate interest in SAF into credible and scalable demand.

Building this demand is particularly important for aviation decarbonisation in Asia, where much of the sector's future growth is expected. SAF supply remains constrained by its premium over conventional jet fuel and production capacity that is still developing. Stronger and clearer demand signals can encourage investment in new supply and help lower the cost of SAF adoption.

SAFc can provide these demand signals at scale by enabling companies to support the use of SAF and claim the associated emission reductions towards their climate targets, even where direct access to physical SAF is limited or impossible. To support the development of a robust SAFc market in Asia-Pacific, GFF will work with industry, policymakers and standards bodies to establish a trusted framework for corporate engagement.

Frederick Teo, CEO, GenZero, said, "Given the growth of aviation in the Asia-Pacific, the region has a critical role in decarbonising aviation globally. There is tremendous potential to develop technologies in SAF, source feedstock, build production capacity and drive adoption. Corporate ambition to address air travel emissions can direct financing into scaling SAF adoption through the purchase of SAF certificates. Green Fuel Forward aggregates corporate participation into credible, collective demand large enough to meaningfully support production growth across the region. The expertise that GMA and SAFCo bring in demand aggregation, procurement, and market development strengthens Green Fuel Forward's broad membership base to translate corporate readiness into concerted market action."

Kim Carnahan, CEO, Center for Green Market Activation, said. "We know that book and claim and demand aggregation can drive new investment and grow the supply of high-integrity SAF. We are thrilled to be joining the Green Fuel Forward SteerCo to bring this model to Asia, ensure it complements existing global initiatives like the Sustainable Aviation Buyers Alliance, and steer it toward real-world contracting that scales SAF uptake in one of the fastest growing aviation markets in the world."

Seow Hui Tan, CEO, SAFCo, said, "As Asia-Pacific's aviation sector continues to grow, the region has a unique opportunity to lead the next phase of sustainable aviation growth. Singapore's early leadership in advancing SAF policy demonstrates how practical regulations, trusted governance, and market-based mechanisms can accelerate SAF adoption while maintaining environmental integrity. Beyond supporting Singapore's national SAF ambitions, SAFCo's expertise, processes, systems, and market infrastructure being developed through the SAF policy can help lay the foundations for a credible and scalable voluntary SAF and SAF certificate market across Asia-Pacific. Through Green Fuel Forward, we look forward to working with partners to strengthen corporate participation, build market confidence, and accelerate the development of a trusted regional SAF ecosystem."

With added institutional expertise and a broader corporate buyer base, GFF is better positioned to help companies move from learning about SAFc to evaluating and participating in procurement opportunities. By aggregating demand and strengthening connections among buyers, market intermediaries and suppliers, GFF aims to create a stronger commercial foundation for SAF growth in Asia.

As GFF moves from capacity-building towards supporting more pragmatic action, WEF will hand over the secretariat function of the initiative to the SteerCo. WEF played an important role in the initiative's formative year, helping to shape the platform, convene stakeholders, build momentum, and strengthen the understanding of the SAF market.

Pedro Gomez, head, industry agenda, member of the executive committee, World Economic Forum, said, "With GenZero and dozens of private sector companies, we launched Green Fuel Forward to spark interest in SAF in the Asia-Pacific region. One and a half years later, this collective effort has shown that the local SAF market is maturing fast, and more corporates are planning to take pragmatic action and invest in the sector. The World Economic Forum looks forward to seeing this momentum transform into credible demand as GenZero and the new SteerCo take over the strategic leadership of the campaign, bringing experience from transactions that can really scale the impact of Green Fuel Forward in the coming years."

title: Syngas, the Perfect Middleman Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
description:

The plant will be one of the first to convert waste into syngas, then transform and refine it into high-quality sustainable fuels.
Fuel will be obtained from municipal solid waste (MSW) and commercial and industrial waste (C&I), thus transforming waste into strategic resources.
Grey hydrogen (from fossil hydrocarbon feedstocks), blue hydrogen (fossil hydrocarbon feedstocks with CCS) or green hydrogen (from biomass or waste) or ammonia are produced.
New frontiers for biohydrogen In the future, the group also envisions the production of syngas from biogas to generate biohydrogen.
text:
In the gas universe, syngas, or synthesis gas – a mixture of gases consisting of hydrogen (H₂), carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂), with trace amounts of methane and water vapour – is attracting increasing attention from major chemical and new fuel producers.

It is not a primary energy source: rather, it is a chemical intermediate derived from natural gas or even biogas, a sort of industrial wild card that can be transformed into many other products, whose nature depends on where it is generated. And this is precisely its strength.

Nowadays, syngas has various uses. It can be employed as a direct energy source to power turbines. It can generate “synthetic” diesel and jet fuel through Fischer-Tropsch synthesis. It can be utilised for hydrogen production with all its derivatives, both in chemical processes and as a potential carrier, and be highly decarbonised. Furthermore, it is a truly important intermediate for the synthesis of compounds that may become relevant for decarbonisation, for methanol, for low-carbon fertilisers and for decarbonised marine fuels such as ammonia, and it can even be obtained from the gasification or pyrolysis of plastic waste to fuel productive recycling “from waste to energy”.

In order to maximise its role as an intermediate in decarbonisation processes, it is necessary to pay attention to the sources from which syngas is synthesised. “Currently, the main initiatives are still focused on traditional fossil raw materials, placing a strong emphasis on emissions mitigation and efficiency, thus reducing the amount of fossil feedstock used to produce the same amount of product,” explains Menica Antonelli, Incremental Innovation Head of Department at KT Tech, Nextchem (MAIRE group), a leading player in the sector for the creation of new technologies and plant construction.

Syngas for decarbonisation

Long term, however, the outlook changes significantly. Even in the oil and gas sector, work is ongoing on alternative processes for generating syngas without the use of fossil fuels. “In recent years, we have seen a sharp deceleration. The technologies exist or are under development, but a suitable international regulatory framework is still needed. For many operators, the course has been set.” According to Maire's experts, these technologies have a future, but they need to find an economic optimum via both market and regulatory mechanisms.

This does not mean that low-carbon technologies and projects are not being developed. For example, there is a lot of interest in producing syngas using non-recyclable inorganic and organic waste. Last year, the subsidiary Nextchem signed a design contract with Altalto Ltd for a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant in Immingham, Lincolnshire, UK. The plant will be one of the first to convert waste into syngas, then transform and refine it into high-quality sustainable fuels. The initiative, expected to be operational in 2030, will produce 30 million litres of SAF per year (equivalent to approximately 23,000 tonnes), in line with the UK's SAF Mandate aimed at reducing emissions in the aviation sector. Fuel will be obtained from municipal solid waste (MSW) and commercial and industrial waste (C&I), thus transforming waste into strategic resources.

Syngas for hydrogen

“Another area of interest is hydrogen, which has various significant uses,” explains Paolo Mazzara, Commercial & Business Development Head of Department at KT Tech. Syngas, in fact, contains carbon monoxide and hydrogen; the hydrogen concentration is increased by causing the carbon monoxide to react with water vapour in a process called water-gas shift (WGS). Grey hydrogen (from fossil hydrocarbon feedstocks), blue hydrogen (fossil hydrocarbon feedstocks with CCS) or green hydrogen (from biomass or waste) or ammonia are produced.

“As far as blue hydrogen is concerned, one of the largest projects we have contributed to is in the port of Antwerp with the American industrial gas giant Air Products, a major producer and supplier of technical gases,” continues Mazzara. “Here, the proximity of old depleted oil fields in the North Sea made it possible to inject CO2 removed from the process at a relatively low cost, rendering this project economically competitive. This shows how crucial it is to carefully assess the resources available in the area when choosing processes.”

Among the technologies to produce low-carbon blue hydrogen is NX eBlue, a process based on electrified steam methane reforming (eSMR) and developed by Nextchem through its subsidiary KT Tech. “This technology, previously applied in a project in the United States, significantly reduces CO₂ production and integrates carbon capture to further minimise emissions, providing operational flexibility and scalability. We are very proud of this achievement, which places Nextchem at the forefront of the electrification of the hydrogen production process from hydrocarbons,” concludes Antonelli.

New frontiers for biohydrogen

In the future, the group also envisions the production of syngas from biogas to generate biohydrogen. The direct conversion of renewable gas into bio-LNG or biomethane is very energy-intensive, with reduced overall efficiency, high industrial costs and less flexibility of use compared to intermediate conversion into syngas. “It is not that the conversion of biogas into syngas and therefore biohydrogen is absolutely competitive in terms of costs compared to direct conversion into LNG, but it is likely that new subsidies will emerge over time,” adds Mazzara. “We believe that two competitive trends will emerge: in areas with a high concentration of biomass, it will be converted into biohydrogen via syngas, whereas in more localised production areas, LNG production will become inevitable.”

The possibilities therefore remain wide open. The future of syngas as an intermediate will be determined by a mix of market forces, regulations and industrial strategies linked to a new phase in chemistry and advanced decarbonisation plants.

title: How FedEx's CSO engineers sustainability into long-term strategy - Trellis Group
description:
