title: Green Skies or Greenwashing? A Critical Systematic Review of Airline Sustainability Claims ...
authors: Pooja Singh Pooja Singh, Nayhel Sharma Nayhel Sharma
description:
Methods: This critical systematic review collates the research regarding airline sustainability claims, greenwashing, environmental credibility, passenger trusts in and willingness to pay for green air travel.
Based on this literature, the study has considered five analytical dimensions: claim transparency, perceived greenwashing, source credibility, passenger trust and willingness to pay.
Results: Literature reports that sustainability communication is likely to elicit positive responses from consumers if it is credible, reliable and verifiable and specific.
The review suggests a Green Airline Credibility-Trust-TP (GACT-WTP) framework which connects the specificity of the claims, the quality of evidence, feelings of greenwashing and finally, credibility and passenger trust and willingness to pay.
The framework sees credibility as the key enabler of the transformation of sustainability communication into economic value-or its lack thereof.
text:
Abstract

Background: To assess the effectiveness of the strategies used to achieve this. Rationale: Aviation is facing ever-greater pressure to reduce its environmental footprint, while still meeting passenger demand and commercial viability. So, airlines use these assertions about sustainable aviation fuel, carbon offsets, fleet efficiency, emissions reduction and waste reduction, as well as net-zero commitments, to communicate sustainability. Such statements are, however, increasingly disputed as the credibility of environmental communication can be undermined by the focus on selective benefits and the hiding of absolute emission, uncertainty and the limits of mitigation. Methods: This critical systematic review collates the research regarding airline sustainability claims, greenwashing, environmental credibility, passenger trusts in and willingness to pay for green air travel. Based on this literature, the study has considered five analytical dimensions: claim transparency, perceived greenwashing, source credibility, passenger trust and willingness to pay. Specific focus is on the airline-specific evidence, communication on carbon-offsets, sustainable aviation fuel and green advertising and consumer research recently conducted. Results: Literature reports that sustainability communication is likely to elicit positive responses from consumers if it is credible, reliable and verifiable and specific. On the other hand, ambiguous and hyperbole or compensation-based claims may lead to an impression of “greenwashing” and lower brand assessments, behavioral intentions and trust. There is a willingness on the part of passengers to pay for environmental improvements but this is subject to the credibility, size and transparency of the environmental benefit. There is recent evidence from meta-analysis that offsetting schemes with a high degree of credibility can elicit significantly higher willingness to pay than schemes of lower credibility. Conclusion: The conclusion, then, is not that claims of sustainability are being made by airlines, it's that there is a credibility gap between the air industry's self-reported environmental performance and real environmental results. The review suggests a Green Airline Credibility-Trust-TP (GACT-WTP) framework which connects the specificity of the claims, the quality of evidence, feelings of greenwashing and finally, credibility and passenger trust and willingness to pay. The framework sees credibility as the key enabler of the transformation of sustainability communication into economic value-or its lack thereof.

Date

(MENAFN- Bangladesh Monitor) Dhaka: American express logistics giant FedEx is expanding its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) procurement through fresh agreements expected to secure more than 20 million gallons of neat SAF across five US airports through 2027.

The deals cover FedEx operations at Newark Liberty International (EWR), Oakland International (OAK), Miami International (MIA), John F. Kennedy International (JFK), and Dallas Fort Worth International (DFW) airports, with blend ratios expected to range from 30% to 50% depending on location.

The multinational conglomerate is working towards a goal of sourcing 30% of its jet fuel from alternative blends by 2030, as part of a broader push to expand SAF use across its US air network.

"The latest agreements represent an expansion of SAF within the FedEx air network enabled, in part, by state and federal level incentives," said Greg Paulus, Vice President of Enterprise Sourcing, in a statement on September 15.

Since 2025, FedEx has secured roughly 5 million gallons of neat SAF, which resulted in the deployment of 16.5 million gallons of blended SAF across the same five airports.

With the newest procurement phase, SAF blends will account for a significant share of FedEx's jet fuel use at those locations.

"SAF is one of the most impactful decarbonization solutions available to aviation today and an important part of our approach to reducing emissions," said Karen Blanks Ellis, Chief Sustainability Officer and Vice President of Environmental Affairs at FedEx.

Ellis added that growing the market requires supply that is reliable, affordable, and sustainable, and that expanding procurement helps boost both usage and demand for greater production and scale.

FedEx said the new agreements mark another step toward wider SAF adoption across its network, and it will continue exploring opportunities as supply, infrastructure, and economics permit further expansion.

text:
September 21, 2026

Velocys has expanded its Fischer-Tropsch reactor roadmap with AlphaCore™ 800, its highest-capacity microchannel FT reactor to date and a product designed specifically for the larger sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and e-fuels projects now emerging globally.

AlphaCore 800 is designed to produce up to 800 barrels per day, or approximately 30 kt/a, of Fischer-Tropsch liquids from a single reactor. It extends the AlphaCore product family from approximately 50 to 800 barrels per day per reactor and is particularly suited to SAF plants targeting 100+ kt/a of production.

The objective behind the AlphaCore roadmap is straightforward: more FT capacity per reactor, enabling fewer reactors as project scale increases.

For project developers, reducing reactor count can simplify the Fischer-Tropsch island, reduce associated equipment requirements and lower FT unit cost while building on Velocys’ established microchannel technology platform and operating experience.

The effect becomes increasingly significant as projects grow. An FT unit requiring approximately 1,600 barrels per day, or 60 kt/a, of FT liquids could use two AlphaCore 800 reactors instead of eight AlphaCore 200 reactors, a 75% reduction in reactor count for the same FT liquids capacity.

AlphaCore 800 joins AlphaCore 50, 200 and 400 to create a throughput-based Fischer-Tropsch reactor family using the same core technology across multiple project scales and syngas pathways.

The new reactor is being announced as the sustainable fuels industry gathers in Hong Kong for Sustainable Aviation Futures China, where developers, technology providers and investors are considering the next generation of commercial-scale SAF and e-fuels projects across China and the wider Asian market.

text:
Emerson has been awarded a contract by Technip Energies to provide automation technologies for the SkyNRG sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant—the first dedicated greenfield SAF production facility in Europe. Emerson’s DeltaV integrated control and safety system (ICSS) will help ensure safe, reliable startup and long-term operational performance, while reducing project risk for this first-of-its-kind facility.

Currently under construction in Delfzijl, the new SAF facility will support the Netherlands' efforts to meet the EU's sustainable aviation fuel mandate. Once fully operational in 2028, the facility is expected to produce approximately 100,000 metric tons of SAF annually. The plant will convert residual fats and greases into a sustainable “drop-in” fuel that can be blended with conventional jet fuel without requiring modifications to aircraft or fueling infrastructure. The project will also support compliance with the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, which requires all jet fuel supplied at EU airports to contain a minimum of 2% SAF from 2025, rising to 70% by 2050.

“Developing Europe’s first dedicated sustainable aviation fuel facility is a major step in scaling SAF production and supporting aviation decarbonization,” said Bart Rosendaal, site director of DSL-01 at SkyNRG. “Working with experienced partners like Technip Energies and Emerson helps ensure we can deliver a safe, reliable and future-ready plant from day one.”

As a greenfield facility, the plant will be born digital, with advanced automation technologies implemented from the outset to ensure efficient, reliable and safe operations. The ICSS will include Emerson’s DeltaV Distributed Control System and DeltaV Safety Instrumented System, providing process control, safety shutdown and fire and gas detection. Emerson’s AMS Device Manager plant asset management software will support efficient commissioning and ongoing maintenance by delivering device data, health insights and advanced diagnostics from intelligent field devices.

These systems will manage all process units, including the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids process to produce SAF, an advanced feedstock pre-treatment unit and an on-site hydrogen plant based on Technip Energies’ proprietary high efficiency steam methane reforming technology. Together, they will provide real-time visibility and stable, consistent operation of the facility, helping to improve reliability and optimize throughput.

text:
Sasol is the world’s biggest producer of fuel and chemicals made from coal, and one of South Africa’s heaviest emitters. That makes what it announced on 15 September an odd sentence to write. At the Africa Green Hydrogen Summit in Cape Town it said it had sold its first commercial volumes of sustainable aviation fuel, made from used cooking oil at its Natref refinery, to a company called White Desert.

White Desert flies holidaymakers from Cape Town to Antarctica, and has used low-carbon fuel since 2021. Nothing new was built to supply it. The waste oil goes into Natref, Sasol’s refinery at Sasolburg, and comes out as fuel that meets flight specification, and it counts as low-carbon because the refinery recently earned a sustainability certificate. Sarushen Pillay, who runs business building and strategy at Sasol, says aviation gets cleaner by transforming the industrial plants that already exist, not abandoning them.

Someone has to pay for it first. Sustainable aviation fuel can cost 2 to 3 times more than conventional jet fuel, which makes White Desert an interesting first customer. A one-day flight from Cape Town to Antarctica costs $16,500, with a glacier abseil and champagne in an ice bar attached, while a seven-day trip runs to $120,000. Aviation accounts for about 2% of the world’s carbon dioxide emissions, so a few expedition flights are not the dent. Sasol’s near-term focus is still raising output at Secunda, the coal-to-fuel plant that makes it what it is.

text:
Japan Airlines has signed what the companies describe as the world’s first purchase agreement for carbon removal credits designed to meet CORSIA requirements.

Climeworks Solutions will source a portfolio including soil carbon sequestration and biochar, alongside separate Direct Air Capture credits.

The deal offers an early test of how carbon removal could move from voluntary corporate climate strategies into aviation compliance markets.

JAL moves carbon removal into aviation compliance

Japan Airlines has signed a carbon removal agreement with Climeworks Solutions that could open a new route for airlines managing emissions under global aviation rules.

The companies said the pilot is the world’s first purchase agreement for carbon dioxide removal credits designed to meet the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, known as CORSIA.

The agreement brings carbon removal closer to a regulated aviation market. It also creates an early source of demand for removal projects capable of meeting CORSIA’s eligibility requirements.

For airlines, the development comes as the sector faces pressure to cut emissions while managing the limits of current decarbonization technologies. New aircraft, operational efficiencies and Sustainable Aviation Fuel remain central to the transition. Carbon removal could provide another tool for emissions that remain after those measures.

“As the first airline to secure CORSIA-compliant carbon removals, we are proud to lead the industry toward net-zero emissions,” said Noriko Ogawa, Executive Officer and Chairperson, Sustainability Promotion Committee, Japan Airlines. “While reducing emissions through aircraft renewal, operational innovations and the use of SAF remains our top priority, high-integrity carbon removals are essential to address residual emissions. Through this pioneering partnership with Climeworks, we aim to accelerate the adoption of high-quality solutions across international aviation and contribute to a sustainable future for air travel.”

A portfolio approach to carbon removal

Climeworks Solutions will source a portfolio of removal credits intended to fulfil requirements for ICAO CORSIA Eligible Emissions Units.

The portfolio will span different carbon removal pathways, including soil carbon sequestration and biochar. This approach gives JAL access to removal options available at greater scale today while spreading exposure across different technologies and project types.

JAL will separately purchase Direct Air Capture credits from Climeworks. DAC uses engineered systems to capture carbon dioxide directly from ambient air, after which the CO2 can be permanently stored.

The additional purchase is designed to support the development of permanent engineered removals even as JAL uses other pathways for its CORSIA obligations.

RELATED ARTICLE: Japan Airlines Enters into New Fuel Sales Agreement with Gevo for 5.3 Million Gallons of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Per Year Over Five Years

“This agreement with JAL represents an important milestone not only for aviation, but for the wider carbon removal industry,” said Adrian Siegrist, Chief Commercial Officer at Climeworks. “Earlier this year, Climeworks Solutions expanded its offering to help organizations procure carbon removal portfolios aligned with emerging compliance frameworks, including CORSIA. This agreement demonstrates how carbon removal is increasingly moving from voluntary climate action into compliance markets.”

CORSIA creates a new demand channel

CORSIA is ICAO’s global framework for addressing emissions from international aviation. Its requirements create a potentially significant source of demand for eligible carbon credits as airlines manage their compliance obligations.

JAL has already participated in that market. The carrier was among the early airlines to retire large volumes of CORSIA-eligible credits. Its latest agreement extends that activity into carbon dioxide removal.

For the carbon market, the distinction matters. Much of the corporate demand for carbon removal has historically come through voluntary climate commitments. Integrating removals into compliance frameworks could broaden the buyer base and create more predictable demand.

It could also increase scrutiny. Buyers will need to assess durability, measurement, verification and environmental integrity alongside regulatory eligibility. Those considerations become more consequential when credits are used to satisfy formal compliance requirements rather than voluntary targets.

Aviation tests the role of permanent removals

JAL’s strategy continues to prioritize direct emissions reductions through fleet renewal, operational improvements and SAF. Carbon removal is positioned as a tool for residual emissions rather than a substitute for those measures.

That distinction will be important as aviation works toward long-term climate targets. The sector remains difficult to decarbonize because of its dependence on energy-dense fuels and the long operating lives of aircraft.

For executives and investors, the JAL agreement provides an early view of how compliance demand could reshape carbon removal procurement. Airlines may increasingly need to evaluate carbon credits not simply by price, but by regulatory eligibility, durability and supply security.

If CORSIA-compliant removals expand beyond pilot transactions, international aviation could become an important bridge between the voluntary carbon removal market and regulated climate finance. That would give removal developers a new class of buyers while adding another component to airlines’ increasingly complex decarbonization strategies.

Based on ICAO lifecycle values, UCO-based HEFA SAF can achieve an estimated 84% lifecycle emissions reduction compared with conventional jet fuel; At a 5% SAF blend by 2030, India could achieve an estimated 4.2% lifecycle CO emissions reduction versus conventional jet fuel, assuming the SAF is produced through the UCO-based HEFA pathway.

UCO alone cannot meet India's SAF needs. Feedstocks such as crop residues, bagasse, municipal waste, waste fats and oils, sustainable oilseeds and PtL can diversify supply and support farmer incomes. The objective is to build a transparent and traceable supply chain from kitchen and farm to refinery and certified SAF production.

"India's SAF programme will depend not only on technology, but on building credible and traceable feedstock supply chains. Connecting the kitchen and farm to the refinery can unlock important domestic resources for India's SAF transition."

Byufuel currently collects UCO from food businesses across 70+ Indian cities and supplies it to refineries through certified supply chains supported by digital chain-of-custody systems.

text:
Houston, Texas-based company Velocys has launched AlphaCore 800, its newest reactor that uses Fisher-Tropsch (FT) technology to produce upto 800 barrels of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) every day. AlphaCore 800 joins Velocys’ fleet of reactors and promises more output per reactor without a drop in performance or reliability.

As countries look to move away from fossil fuels, renewable and nuclear energy adoption is on the rise. While these technologies solve the problem of not letting more carbon into the atmosphere without sacrificing the energy demand, there are specific applications that they simply cannot serve.

High-octane fossil fuels can be burnt to generate short bursts of energy needed for large aircraft takeoff, which neither renewable nor nuclear energy can match. To continue using these modes of transport, we need an alternative fuel that matches the energy density of fossil fuels but not their carbon footprint. This is where synthetic fuel made using the Fischer-Tropsch process comes in handy.

What is the Fischer-Tropsch process?

Fischer-Tropsch (FT) is a complex chemical process that turns syngas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, into liquid hydrocarbon fuel. First developed nearly a century ago, the FT process passes a syngas, or synthesis gas, over a metal catalyst such as iron or cobalt under high heat and pressure to polymerize into long-chain hydrocarbons.

This results in a synthetic crude oil that can be further refined and used a fuel for cars, trucks and even airplanes. The reason this approach is considered sustainable is that it does not tap into the underground crude oil reserves. Instead, it uses carbon dioxide that already exists in the atmosphere and binds it into a fuel, which is burnt again, so it does not add to the planet’s emissions.

More from Energy

See All

FT helps generate replacement fuels for petrol, diesel and aviation fuel without using non-oil sources while also helping convert captured carbon dioxide and green hydrogen into sustainable e-fuels.

How does Velocys generate SAF?

The FT process involves a series of reactions conducted at temperatures between 302-572 degrees Fahrenheit (150-300 degrees Celsius) and several tens of atmospheres of pressure.

Velocys uses microchannel FT reactors and proprietary catalysts to increase fuel yield and make the technology easier to deploy for field use. The company currently has a portfolio of AlphaCore 50,200 and 400 reactors and has now added a high-capacity reactor offering.

“Customers are asking us to bring our microchannel FT technology into larger projects with simpler configurations,” said Matthew Viergutz, CEO of Velocys. “AlphaCore 800 is a direct response. As SAF projects move toward 100,000 tonnes per year and beyond, we are increasing capacity per reactor so developers can configure larger FT plants with fewer units while building on the technology platform and operating experience of Velocys.”

As the name suggests, The AlphaCore 800 doubles the capacity of its predecessor AlphaCore 400 and is designed to produce 800 barrels per day or 30,000 tonnes per year (30 kt/a) of FT output from a single reactor.

Adding more capacity to this offering, Velocys makes it possible for its customers to scale their production while deploying fewer reactors, which simplifies the plant setup, reduces use of associated equipment, and lowers unit cost.

For instance, a facility looking to produce 1,600 barrels of FT fluid per day can now do so using two units of Velocys AlphaCore 800 instead of eight AlphaCore 200 units, reducing reactor count by 75 percent without changing performance or reaction chemistry, a press release said.

text:
Warming temperatures are fueling more extreme weather-related events - catastrophic floods, severe hurricanes and cyclones, and wildfires exacerbated by drought. But the tools used by local communities, emergency and public safety agencies, and insurance and risk markets have not kept pace with the up-to-date data and modeling for accurately predicting how these events will evolve.

Addressing that shortcoming was one of five research areas selected for MIT's 2022 Climate Grand Challenges, an ambitious effort to accelerate science-based solutions to climate problems. The area, titled "Preparing for a New World of Weather and Climate Extremes," focuses on tools to help evaluate a location's vulnerabilities to flooding, cyclones, humid heat waves, or other climate-related events.

Four years later, collaborations among more than 40 faculty and student researchers on Weather and Climate Extremes projects have yielded 29 published research papers and digital tools and datasets that are already in use or close to deployment. Individual projects cut across forecasting, risk assessment, on-the-ground planning, and resilient infrastructure.

"Communities across the United States and around the world are already confronting the consequences of extreme weather," says Evelyn Wang, MIT's vice president for energy and climate, whose office has been funding and supporting all of the Grand Challenges since 2024. "Through the Climate Grand Challenges, an interdisciplinary team at MIT is advancing the science, technologies, and practical strategies needed to help communities anticipate these risks and build greater resilience."

Reducing Scientific Uncertainties

Paul O'Gorman, the Robert R. Shrock Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences at MIT and co-lead of Weather and Climate Extremes, is refining the science behind forecasting extreme weather events, such as last year's major flooding events in Central Texas and in Pakistan. "There have been a lot of unprecedented, record-breaking events," he says, "and we want to understand how they are changing as the climate warms, and how they're changing in different regions."

One aspect that his group has been examining is the relationship between extreme rainfall events and a warming climate. Climate models predict that extreme rainfall increases less in summer than other seasons in much of the United States and Europe. O'Gorman's team found that these seasonal shifts stem from not only how much water is in the atmosphere, which is measured by specific humidity, but also how close it is to saturation, which is measured by relative humidity. "We found that changes in relative humidity played a big role, which was something that hadn't been appreciated before, and something we need to take into account," he says.

Modeling is challenging: Relative humidity depends on air circulation, how fast land warms relative to the ocean, soil moisture, and vegetation. "It's a complex story, but this helps us understand precipitation patterns," O'Gorman says.

Kerry Emanuel, MIT professor of atmospheric science who was also a co-lead of Weather and Climate Extremes, is researching better ways to estimate the risks of extreme hurricanes and severe convective storms, such as thunderstorms and tornadoes. "For hurricanes, we're pretty much there. We can reproduce the statistics of real hurricanes extremely well just using coarse-grained weather data that has no hurricanes in it," he says. But for severe convective storms, "we're not close to being there," and these storms "in the last decade have cost more lives and more damage than hurricanes."

Research on the physics of storms is already influencing practice, Kerry notes. For example, a company called First Street uses Kerry's methods to guide local governments, insurers, developers, and real-estate platforms on environmental risk for every piece of private property in the United States.

Improving Resilience

Another phase of the Grand Challenge, led by Miho Mazereeuw, an associate professor in MIT's Department of Architecture and a leading expert on resilient design, translates the information from scientific modeling and data collection into tools for on-the-ground planners. For example, working with leaders and community members in Boston and Broward County, Florida, the team has developed interactive web-based tools that make it easier to plan for impacts such as flooding over a broad range of scenarios.

"When an extreme event happens, there is a gap between scientific knowledge and actionable public information," says Aditya Barve, a research scientist in Mazereeuw's Urban Risk Lab. This happens at various levels - from getting real-time information out to people when they need it to collecting data to enable long-term planning to disseminating those plans to communities. "The idea is to target the gap through tools in community emergency data collection, proactive recovery planning, and AI-assisted tools for at-scale visualization of future climate impacts, so that communities are prepared when something happens."

The team has worked on making flood modeling outputs usable by a wider range of stakeholders, especially where the need for specialized software or technical expertise can slow decision-making across city departments. "Users can ask practical questions, such as which schools are likely to stay driest across different flood scenarios, and receive answers grounded in flood models and city datasets within seconds," Barve says.

As for recovery after extreme weather events, Mazereeuw points out that most municipalities have an emergency response plan, but few create a recovery plan that includes housing before the event. But, she says, if communities plan how recovery can lead to a better future for the city, they can better leverage emergency relief funding that becomes available. "In almost all cases, the resources available after a disaster are much larger," she says. "By having a plan in place, those resources can fit the vision of the place moving forward."

Optimizing Energy Infrastructure

Associate Professor Michael Howland is working to analyze the impacts of extreme weather on energy infrastructure with a team that includes Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS), and Moshe Ben-Akiva, the Edmund K. Turner Professor in Civil Engineering at MIT. The team is particularly looking at impacts on the electrical power system and ways to optimize decisions on the placement and sizing of new energy infrastructure.

Howland, who is the Jeffrey Cheah Career Development Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at MIT, says electrical power systems are increasingly being altered by two things at the same time: first, the proliferation of renewable energy and storage technologies, and second, large-scale changes in weather and extreme events driven by climate change. "Each of these would independently push our electrical power system potentially outside of what we are used to, and their combined, synergistic impacts could be even larger because they are occurring simultaneously," he says.

Bringing climate modeling and grid-infrastructure work together has accelerated practical insights into how we can adapt to climate change while simultaneously mitigating it, Howland notes. Such modeling can also help to inform infrastructure decisions in ways that may not be obvious. For example, he says, their optimization model for the siting of power resources in Texas resulted in placing a number of wind power plants along the Gulf Coast. "If you look at an average wind speed map," he says, "you would say this doesn't make much sense because it's really windy in northwest Texas on average, and much less windy along the Gulf Coast."

But it turns out that the typical daily cycle of winds is complementary, so that wind farms distributed between both locations tend to smooth each other out and to better complement solar power generation, easing burdens on the grid. Now, "we're trying to take it further not just by smoothing the generation, but actually aligning it with the time- and space-varying electricity demand so that we can reduce storage, transmission, and other backup generation needs," he says.

This work is ongoing, and the hope is that it will lead to products that can directly help utility grid planners and regulators with actionable information about the siting and sizing of various electrical infrastructure resources, Howland says. "We want to continuously push on model realism and accuracy to eventually make it more of a practical and useful tool for grid planners."

Emanuel adds that the Weather and Climate Extremes Grand Challenge, and other projects working to pinpoint the kinds of risks that can be expected from a changing climate, have produced a great deal of specific and detailed information that could guide political, economic, and civic decision-making. Applying it in the real world can be a slow - "like steering a supertanker," he says - but progress will come.

text:
Methane-to-SAF pathway combines Infinium's commercially deployed advanced Fischer–Tropsch platform with electrified reforming to expand where low-carbon aviation fuel can be produced

SACRAMENTO, Calif., Sept. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Infinium today introduced its mSAF product offering, a new methane-derived sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) platform which converts renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas, and other qualified methane streams into low-carbon aviation fuel. The new offering expands the feedstocks and locations available for Infinium projects while complementing the company's growing CO₂-based eSAF business.

The expansion addresses a fundamental challenge for aviation: no single feedstock pathway can produce all of the low-carbon fuel needed to satisfy rising SAF mandates and industry commitments. Renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas and other methane streams are already aggregated at landfills, dairies, wastewater facilities and gas-gathering systems across North America, Asia, Europe and other geographies and are increasingly looking for diversified end use opportunities.

"mSAF expands what Infinium's platform can do. It gives us another way to apply our proven technology, develop projects across a broader range of locations and deliver more low-carbon fuel alongside our growing eSAF business. Aviation needs multiple scalable pathways, and Infinium is positioned to continue to deliver options."

— Robert Schuetzle, CEO, Infinium

One Proven Technology, Two Feedstock Pathways

Infinium has more than a decade of experience converting gases into liquid hydrocarbons with its synthesis technology deployed across commercial installations. Synthesize™ — Infinium's proprietary advanced Fischer–Tropsch catalyst and reactor design for converting syngas into liquid hydrocarbons — is also used to produce Infinium eFuels today. The two product lines share core synthesis technology, catalyst manufacturing, product specifications and certification pathways.

Electrified Reforming Improves Yield and Carbon Performance

Infinium's mSAF platform also utilizes its proprietary Reform™ package - a proprietary electric steam methane reformer (eSMR) designed to produce syngas with a lower carbon footprint than a traditional gas-fired SMR. Infinium is deploying the world's largest eSMR at Project Roadrunner, for conversion of methane into syngas.

Conventional steam methane reforming burns a portion of the feed gas to produce process heat. This adds combustion emissions to the fuel's lifecycle footprint and consumes feedstock carbon that could otherwise be converted into the finished product.

Infinium's Reform™ technology uses renewable electricity to provide that process heat. This keeps more feedstock carbon available for conversion, increasing fuel yield per unit of gas, while avoiding the reforming-related combustion emissions associated with conventional systems. For RNG projects, where feedstock cost and carbon intensity are central to commercial performance, greater yield and lower reforming emissions directly improve project economics.

Carbon Intensity Verified Project by Project

Infinium worked with RMI, an independent energy and climate research organization with expertise in methane emissions, low-carbon fuels, aviation and industrial decarbonization, on an assessment of the growing mSAF market opportunity.

"Biogas and renewable natural gas are emerging as important areas of inquiry for hard-to-abate sectors, including low-carbon fuels and industrial value chains. These pathways may offer meaningful climate and commercial value, but only if they are supported by rigorous lifecycle accounting, auditable chain-of-custody systems, and credible certification frameworks. RMI was pleased to support Infinium's strategic assessment of this evolving landscape to better understand challenges and opportunities for meaningful climate benefit."

- Bryan Fisher, Managing Director, RMI

The mSAF designation does not imply a single carbon-intensity value across all projects. Lifecycle emissions will depend on the methane source, leakage rate, production-energy mix and chain of custody on individual assets. Infinium will calculate and independently certify carbon intensity at the project level under applicable regulatory and voluntary certification frameworks.

By adding mSAF to its eFuels platform, Infinium is expanding the range of feedstocks and locations available for low-carbon fuel production while continuing to advance its CO₂-based eSAF business.

Infinium's Project Pathfinder in Corpus Christi, Texas has operated since 2023 as the world's first commercial-scale power-to-liquids eFuels facility. Project Roadrunner is under construction in Pecos, Texas. In collaboration with businesses, policymakers, funders, communities, and other partners, RMI drives investment to scale clean energy solutions, reduce energy waste, and boost access to affordable clean energy in ways that enhance security, strengthen the economy, and improve people's livelihoods. text:
Rolls-Royce has been selected by the European Union’s Clean Aviation programme to lead a project aimed at demonstrating hybrid-electric propulsion technology for future short- and medium-range aircraft, as the aviation industry seeks to cut emissions while improving fuel efficiency.

The ELEVATED project is one of 19 initiatives selected under the latest Clean Aviation funding call. The projects will receive up to €290 million in EU funding and are expected to generate total public and private investment of €664 million, supporting technologies ranging from hybrid-electric propulsion to hydrogen-powered and ultra-efficient regional aircraft.

Led by Rolls-Royce Deutschland, the ELEVATED consortium includes industrial, academic and research partners from France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain and the United Kingdom. The partners will work on areas including hybridisation, electrification, engine integration, electrical machines and drives, high-voltage systems, aircraft integration and technology modelling.

Subject to the completion of the grant process, the project will integrate a hybrid-electric subsystem into an existing “donor” engine. The system will then be integrated, controlled and tested under conditions intended to replicate those encountered in aircraft operation.

Rolls-Royce said the hybrid-electric system is being developed towards a target of reducing aircraft-level carbon dioxide emissions by at least 20%.

The project will also assess the potential contribution of hybrid-electric technology to the company’s UltraFan 30 technology demonstrator, supporting its development towards Technology Readiness Level 6, a stage at which technology is considered sufficiently mature for demonstration in a relevant environment.

UltraFan is Rolls-Royce’s next-generation geared engine programme for both narrow-body and wide-body aircraft. The UltraFan 30 demonstrator is focused on short- and medium-range aircraft and is scheduled for ground testing in 2028.

The demonstrator combines new engine-core architecture, fan technology, advanced materials and manufacturing processes, with the aim of improving fuel efficiency, emissions and durability. Rolls-Royce said the engine is being designed to operate with 100% sustainable aviation fuel from the outset.

The ELEVATED project forms part of wider European efforts to develop lower-emission aviation technologies while maintaining the competitiveness of the region’s aerospace industry.

text:
OMV Petrom is advancing the construction of the new sustainable fuels production unit at Petrobrazi. The 560 million euros investment will position the refinery as the first major producer of sustainable fuels in the region. The foundations have been laid, and the main equipment for processing sustainable fuels – including columns and reactors – has been mounted and installed.

With a capacity of 250,000 tonnes per year, the new unit will produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel, fuels that can contribute to reducing emissions in hard-to-electrify sectors such as aviation and heavy transport.

“Petrobrazi is going through one of the most important transformations in its recent history. With a EUR 560 million investment, we are building a new unit that will produce 250,000 tonnes per year of sustainable fuels made from renewable feedstocks. These lower carbon fuels will contribute to reducing emissions in sectors where electrification is difficult, such as aviation and heavy transport. We have completed the foundations, for which approximately 20,000 cubic meters of concrete were poured, and equipment up to 60 meters high is already installed in the refinery. This is a project through which we are gradually adapting Petrobrazi to the new requirements of the market and of the energy transition, including through the development of sustainable fuels production,” said Radu Căprău, member of the OMV Petrom Executive Board.

The new SAF/HVO unit will transform vegetable fats and used cooking oils — renewable feedstocks — with the help of green hydrogen, into fuels similar to conventional ones, but with significantly lower life-cycle emissions.

Construction works started in 2025. In the coming period, works will continue with the installation of equipment, the connection of the new units to the refinery’s existing infrastructure, as well as an extensive testing and verification program before commissioning, estimated for 2028.

At the same time, the company has developed green hydrogen production capacity at Petrobrazi. This year, the modules for the two electrolyzers, with a total capacity of 55 MW, were delivered. The investment in these projects amounts to around 190 million euro.

None of this means U.S. ethanol exporters are headed for a downturn.
text:
U.S. ethanol exports hit a record in 2025, but the federal government's new plan for sustaining that growth reads more like a list of priorities than an outlook. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) American Biofuels Trade Outlook, released September 16, sets out four pillars. Those are increasing on-road ethanol blending, reducing restrictions on crop based biofuels, reaching untapped markets and accelerating opportunities with international bodies such as the United Nations aviation and maritime organizations. The document itself confirms what its four pages suggest. Each pillar carries a short list of actions, but none of them comes with an export projection, a country level demand estimate, a funding commitment or a deadline.

The underlying numbers are strong enough that the gap is worth noticing. USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service credits American farmers with shipping 2.2 billion gallons of ethanol worth $4.7 billion in 2025, a second consecutive record. Growth Energy, an ethanol industry group, and the Renewable Fuels Association, an ethanol trade association, cite similar figures and put the buyer base at nearly 90 countries. Momentum carried into 2026 too. Through June, USDA's own trade data show exports running 12% ahead of last year's record pace by volume and 21% ahead by value.

Canada's Clean Fuel Policy Is Driving Most of the Export Growth

Canada remains the foundation of the export market and typically takes more than a third of U.S. ethanol shipments. Exports there reached a record 3.1 billion liters in 2025, and the growth traces back to regulation rather than a sales push. Canadian fuel ethanol consumption grew more than 50% between 2021 and 2025, driven by the national Clean Fuel Regulations plus provincial blending mandates and low-carbon fuel standards in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, according to USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service. That growth is real, but it leaves U.S. exporters dependent on the durability of one government's carbon policy. A future change to Canada's rules could remove demand as quickly as the regulation created it.

UK Tariff Relief Already Closed the Country's Last Ethanol Plants

The UK opened a separate opportunity after last year's U.S.-UK Prosperity Deal eliminated a 19% tariff on as much as 1.4 billion liters of U.S. ethanol. In May 2025, the Associated British Foods warned at the time that tariff-free imports threatened its Vivergo plant. USDA's trade data confirm the warning proved accurate. The two plants that had produced virtually all UK ethanol closed in mid-to-late 2025. That leaves the UK almost entirely reliant on imports today, which is good for U.S. volume in the near term but removes the domestic buffer that once existed there if trade terms shift again.

Vietnam's New E10 Mandate Is Already Reshaping Trade Flows

Vietnam is the market USDA's blending priority fits best, and the effect showed up almost immediately. The country's nationwide E10 mandate took effect in June and eliminated pure fossil gasoline from sale. USDA projects 2026 fuel ethanol consumption there will run more than eight times last year's level, with domestic production covering only about a quarter of that demand. U.S. exports to Vietnam already reflect the shift, reaching 73 million liters through the first half of 2026, also roughly eight times the full-year 2025 total. Nebraska's ethanol industry recently joined a state trade mission promoting low-carbon ethanol to buyers in Japan and the Philippines, two markets moving through similar transitions.

India, Indonesia and Guatemala Show New Markets Aren't Interchangeable

Not every blending mandate translates into an opening for U.S. suppliers. Imported ethanol cannot be used in India's gasoline-blending program, so American product instead supplies industrial customers there while Indian producers redirect their own ethanol into fuel. Meaningful access to India's E20 market would require a policy change that has not happened. Indonesia looks promising on paper but has already slipped once. Its E10 target was pushed back to 2028 after supply and infrastructure gaps stalled earlier goals.

Guatemala shows a third pattern. A new trade negotiation produced a national E10 mandate that began rolling out in late June, but Guatemala already produces enough ethanol to meet it and is expected to keep exporting its own supply to the EU at a premium while importing cheaper U.S. corn-based ethanol to fill the mandate instead, USDA's trade data show, a wrinkle that only shows up once a market actually opens.

Brazil's Corn Ethanol Boom Is the Biggest Competitive Risk

The largest threat to sustained U.S. growth sits outside the priorities USDA listed at all. Brazil's share of global ethanol exports fell from 23% between 2020 and 2023 to just 12% in 2025, while the U.S. share grew from 48% to 64% over the same stretch. That shift happened because strong domestic Brazilian demand, not weak production, absorbed the country's growing ethanol output. Corn based ethanol accounted for more than 25% of Brazil's total production in the 2025-26 season, up from about 5% six years earlier, and Rabobank projects an additional 3 billion liters of corn ethanol capacity there by the end of 2026. If Brazilian domestic consumption growth slows even slightly, that expanding supply has somewhere to go, and U.S. exporters would be competing on price against a producer with shorter shipping distances to much of Latin America and parts of Asia.

Middle East Conflict and a New Tax Credit Add Fresh 2026 Wildcards

Two developments outside USDA's four pillars could move the numbers further than anything in the outlook itself. High energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have already pushed several countries to adjust biofuel policy on short notice. Brazil temporarily raised its mandatory ethanol blend rate to 32% for 180 days starting in July, which increases domestic consumption and could tighten the supply Brazil has left to export. The Philippines took the opposite path, giving its president authority to temporarily reduce or suspend fuel taxes and blend mandates if energy prices run high enough.

On the U.S. side, modifications to the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) extended the credit's expiration date through December 31, 2029. Crucially, the law removed the Indirect Land Use Change (ILUC) penalty from emissions calculations—a clause that previously penalized crop-based biofuels and would have kept many ethanol producers from claiming the maximum credit value. Additionally, by restricting eligibility exclusively to North American-grown feedstocks, these updates heavily shield the domestic industry, ultimately supporting higher U.S. production and driving more competitive pricing in global export markets.

A separate UK government grant to reopen one shuttered ethanol plant for carbon dioxide production, also a response to Middle East driven energy pressure, could work in the opposite direction by giving European buyers a subsidized domestic alternative to U.S. imports.

None of this means U.S. ethanol exporters are headed for a downturn. USDA's own trade data, published separately from the outlook, already track exactly the pressures that matter most. Those are Canada's policy durability, Brazil's production trajectory, and how quickly new mandates in Vietnam and Guatemala convert into contracted volume.

What the roadmap released September 16 does not do is turn any of that tracking into a forecast, a target or a deadline.

text:
Airbus is investing £150m (US$200.7m) to convert its former A380 wing production facility in Broughton, UK into a dedicated A321 line.

It expects the site to be fully operational by the end of 2026.

Around 480 new high-value jobs will be created at Broughton, with 250 in the refurbished factory joining an existing workforce of 6,000.

The investment supports Airbus' push toward rate 75, a target of 75 A320 Family aircraft per month that would mark the highest production level in civil aerospace history.

Jerome Blandin, Head of Airbus Wing, says: “Investing in our capacity strengthens our industrial footprint, creates high value jobs that support the wider UK aerospace sector and ensures we remain competitive in the years to come.”

Inside Airbus’ UK investment

Once the investment and upgrades are complete, the facility will host six wing production jigs, an equipping line and a paint shop, designed to feed the backlog of around 7,500 A320 Family aircraft.

Airbus says around 70% of its backlogged fleet are A321s, driving almost all of the company’s narrowbody demand.

All of the facility’s production jigs are expected to be in operation by the end of 2026, with the first wing already underway.

The investment follows a separate, recently announced expansion at Airbus' Belfast facility supporting A220 ramp-up.

Airbus says the heart of this investment is a “new, advanced manufacturing environment, designed and built with direct involvement from operators across the site”.

Airbus’ rate 75 strategy

Broughton's expansion aims to improve Airbus' broader production strategy and meet the company’s rate 75 ambition.

Rate 75 is Airbus’s industrial strategy to increase production of its A320neo Family aircraft to 75 jets per month.

Airbus says that its commercial aircraft backlog reached a record 8,754 units in 2025 and the company has already pushed back its rate 75 target once.

In February 2026, Guillaume Faury, Airbus CEO, revealed that a lack of engine supply from Pratt & Whitney has slowed the company’s production down.

The target now sits at reaching between 70 and 75 aircraft a month by the end of 2027, rather than hitting 75 outright.

According to Deloitte's 2026 Aerospace and Defence Industry Outlook, continuing aircraft production backlogs are forcing airlines to fly existing fleets for longer and invest more heavily in maintenance, repair and overhaul.

Aerospace supply chains

Reduced engine supply is not the only factor impacting Airbus’ rate 75 target, as the company’s supply chain was stretched further in December 2025.

During the final month of 2025, Airbus confirmed that it had acquired key Spirit AeroSystems industrial assets, taking over sites in the US, France, Morocco and the UK.

The company received US$439m in compensation, while absorbing more than 4,000 employees.

Components such as fuselage sections and wings for the A220, A320 and A350 were added to Airbus’ production portfolio.

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) issued these recommendations to ensure that the aviation sector covers its own decarbonisation costs if major infrastructure projects—specifically Heathrow Airport’s third runway expansion—are permitted to move forward.

And Jet2 CEO Steve Heapy has strongly criticised recent proposals from the UK government’s advisory body, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warning that steep taxes designed to hit net zero targets will heavily drive up flight costs and turn vacations into the “preserve of the rich”.

The dispute centres around recent CCC findings stating that major projects—like the proposed Heathrow expansion—cannot move forward unless the aviation sector takes drastic measures to clean up emissions.

To fund these targets, the advisory body suggested that the cost of international flights could spike significantly by 2050. Industry bodies estimate that these net zero policies could add around £150 to a family trip to European destinations like Spain.

The independent climate advisory body stated that Heathrow’s planned expansion is “not currently compatible” with the UK’s legal target of reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. To bridge this gap, the CCC recommends that the government legislate a “polluter-pays” framework. This would force the aviation industry to fund cleaner alternatives, such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), and pay for industrial carbon-removal technologies.

Airlines are expected to pass these mitigation costs directly onto passengers. The CCC estimates the gradual financial impact—phased in over the next 25 years leading up to 2050—would equal roughly 6p to 9p per mile, mirroring existing petrol duties.

text:
Key points

Carbon emissions can provide an indirect indication of the transition risk associated with companies financed by banks, according to a senior Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) official.

The HKMA does not currently require banks to disclose financed emissions, which can substantially exceed their direct emissions.

The authority is preparing a separate sustainability disclosure standard for the banking sector for market consultation. Its updated sustainable finance taxonomy adds 24 adaptation-related measures and includes transition pathways for air transport, iron and steel.

The HKMA’s physical risk assessment platform now allows banks to assess assets anywhere in the world under different climate scenarios.

Carbon emissions are a good indicator of the level of physical and transition climate risk that banks are expected to manage, said a senior official from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

“We are not talking about carbon metrics per se, but as the banking regulator for Hong Kong… we expect them to look at physical climate risk and transition climate risk,” said the central bank’s head of sustainable banking development Ronald Young during Hong Kong Green Week in early September.

“The level of transition risk can be indirectly indicated by the level of carbon,” stated Young, adding that higher emissions could suggest higher transition risk in a company financed by a bank.

According to many scientists he has spoken to, Young said that higher temperatures as a result of rising greenhouse gas emissions also raise physical risk, due to heavier rainfall and more vigorous storms.

“Carbon also influences the temperature and in turn influences physical risk,” said Young. “We want [banks] to look at the vulnerabilities and risks, and carbon will give a very good indication in terms of the level of the risk.”

While HKMA does not currently require banks to disclose financed emissions – often 700 times greater than their own direct emissions – a study by the City University of Hong Kong previously estimated that the figure stood at over 380m tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2021.

The central bank primarily addresses climate risks through transition planning guidelines and sustainability disclosure rules aligned with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) framework and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.

On the panel, Young revealed that the central bank is currently working on a separate sustainability disclosure standard for the banking sector, which is expected to be released “sometime by the end of the year or next year” for market consultation.

Green taxonomy updates

HKMA recently launched a public consultation on its updated sustainable finance taxonomy, which was expanded to include 24 more adaptation-related measures that span the water, energy, transportation, buildings, information and communications technology (ICT) as well as risk management sectors.

Under the latest taxonomy, “key enabling technologies” that support the development of several decarbonisation applications, such as the manufacturing and recycling of batteries, can now qualify for financing under the transition label, which was first introduced in January.

Additionally, the updated framework provides transition pathways for certain hard-to-abate sectors, including air transport as well as iron and steel. However, natural gas, nuclear, hydrogen, hydropower, sustainable aviation fuel and carbon capture, usage and storage – which were previously flagged as some areas under consideration in future iterations – remain excluded from the taxonomy.

HKMA’s deputy chief executive Arthur Yuen, who kicked off Hong Kong Green Week with the announcement, said that several banks and corporations have already adopted the taxonomy in their sustainable finance frameworks and begun to issue taxonomy-aligned bonds and loans.

One example he cited was the Bank of China Hong Kong’s recent financing of the jurisdiction’s first public hydrogen refuelling station through a HK$70m (US$8.9m) taxonomy-aligned green loan.

The central bank is working with the industry to build capacity so that “taxonomy alignment becomes the go-to for assessing green and sustainable investment” rather than an exception, said Yuen.

Earlier this year, HKMA also updated the data coverage on its physical risk assessment platform, allowing banks to assess the risk to assets located anywhere in the world under different climate scenarios.

The tool, which was rolled out in 2024, was previously limited to assets within Hong Kong. Since its launch, about 2 million assets have been analysed, said Yuen.

Rolls-Royce to lead EU’s latest clean aviation call

Rolls-Royce has been selected by the European Union’s Clean Aviation programme to lead the ‘Elevated’ project, with the aim of demonstrating a hybrid-electric gas-turbine propulsion system for future ultra-efficient short- to medium-range aircraft.

Elevated is one of 19 groundbreaking Clean Aviation projects announced to further decarbonise aviation while strengthening EU competitiveness and industrial leadership. The initiatives, which also include solutions for hydrogen-powered and ultra-efficient regional aircraft architectures, will receive up to €290 million in EU funding, contributing to a total public and private investment of €664 million across the Clean Aviation Call 4 projects.

The Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking (CAJU) is the European Union’s leading research and innovation programme for transforming aviation towards a sustainable and climate neutral future.

The Rolls-Royce Deutschland-led Elevated consortium brings together key industry, academic and research partners across France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain and the United Kingdom. Together, they contribute unique capabilities across hybridisation, electrification, engine integration, electrical machines and drives, powerplant integration, high-voltage harnesses, aircraft integration, modelling and academic research.

Subject to successful completion of grant preparation, the project will embed a hybrid-electric subsystem into a donor engine, enabling the technology to be integrated, controlled and tested under realistic boundary conditions. The hybrid-electric subsystem is expected to contribute to the ambitious goal of achieving at least a 20% reduction in aircraft-level CO₂ emissions.

Elevated will be used to assess the potential impact of hybrid-electric elements on the UltraFan 30 technology demonstrator and is a key part on the way to Technology Readiness Level 6 (TRL6).

The UltraFan technology programme spans the development of next-generation geared ducted engine solutions for both widebody and narrowbody applications, combining the maturation and validation of novel and proven technologies. UltraFan 30 is Rolls-Royce’s narrowbody technology demonstrator, designed to validate these technologies for future short- and medium-range aircraft.

Planned for ground testing in 2028, it brings together advances in engine core architecture, fan systems, materials and manufacturing to target significant improvements in fuel burn, efficiency, emissions and durability, while being compatible with 100% sustainable aviation fuel from day one.

Alan Newby, Director - Research & Technology, Rolls-Royce, said: “We are proud that Rolls-Royce has been selected to lead the Elevated project as part of the EU’s successful Clean Aviation programme.

By integrating and demonstrating an innovative hybrid-electric system under realistic conditions, we will generate data to validate our modelling and inform technology selection, product development, certification planning and industrialisation. Together with the turbomachinery work being advanced through the ongoing Unified project, it will help bring together the key technology paths needed to validate future UltraFan capability and support best-in-class performance in thrust, fuel burn, noise, emissions and durability.”

In addition to Elevated, Rolls-Royce will also participate in two other Clean Aviation projects announced today: FARMAN (Fuelling Aviation Research for the Management of Advanced distribution systems with hydrogen) and H-ELENA (Hydrogen Engine for Low-Emission NOx Architecture).

title: HK's first five-year plan opens up new opportunities for youth
description:

It proposes making the Youth Development Summit a flagship event for “international youth exchange and collaboration”, while expanding exchanges, internships and practical experiences.
Enhanced employment support, on-the-job training, funding and incubation services, and a housing ladder intended to promote youth home ownership, can help make these opportunities more accessible.
The five-year plan offers a framework to help Hong Kong and its young people navigate change with clearer direction.
The author is a youth ambassador for the Hong Kong Association for External Friendship.
text:
Caleb Hon says employment support, on-the-job training, funding and incubation services, and a housing ladder all offer renewed hope

For young people in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, the most immediate concerns are practical: Where will the next generation of jobs come from? How can an innovative idea become a viable business? Will the skills learned today remain relevant tomorrow? These questions are increasingly pressing as artificial intelligence transforms the labor market, while geopolitical tensions, unilateralism and protectionism create uncertainty for a highly externally-oriented economy. Like students facing an important examination, uncertainty does not disappear and the syllabus remains challenging. What makes a difference is a clear study plan, a realistic timetable and steady progress towards a defined goal. Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan acknowledges the changing environment and addresses issues concerning young people’s education, employment, entrepreneurship and home ownership, while monitoring the impact of technology on the labor market. A coherent five-year strategy is the way forward; it can turn uncertainty into preparation, and preparation into opportunity.

The significance of the plan lies in its medium- to long-term approach. Five years may span a young person’s entire transition from education to employment, professional practice or entrepreneurship. By spelling out “directions of development, mission targets, strategic priorities as well as implementation road maps”, the plan can help educational institutions, employers and young people prepare for future needs with greater confidence. Its implementation framework, “Five-year plan leads, Policy Address implements, Budget supports, annual report gives accounts”, also links long-term objectives with annual policies and public resources, supported by dynamic monitoring, mid-term assessment and final reporting.

Professional services provide one of the clearest examples of the new pathways being opened. Taking the legal industry as a case in point, the plan seeks to deepen Hong Kong’s status as an “international legal and dispute resolution services center”, drawing on its distinctive strengths as a Chinese-English bilingual common-law jurisdiction. It supports the Judiciary of the HKSAR in advancing the establishment of the International Commercial Court, calls for arbitration law reform, and promotes arbitration in specialized fields such as maritime affairs, intellectual property and sport. It also calls for reform of the mediation regulatory system and supports the International Organization for Mediation in furthering its role, with the aim of developing Hong Kong into a “global capital of mediation”.

These developments should be especially encouraging to young practitioners and law students. The plan will enhance and expand the functions of the Hong Kong International Legal Talents Training Academy, which serves as a platform for training, exchanges and the pooling of high-caliber legal talent from around the country and the international community, particularly Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) partner economies. At the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area level, the plan encourages Hong Kong legal talent to take the Greater Bay Area Legal Professional Examination and promotes complementary arbitration regimes, arbitration and mediation standards, and possible model arbitration rules. The Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen and Lau Fau Shan New Development Areas will also prioritize high-end professional services, expressly including finance, insurance, wealth and risk management, legal, mediation, arbitration and accounting services.

The resulting opportunities extend well beyond conventional litigation. Young professionals may increasingly work in cross-border transactions, dispute prevention, specialist arbitration, mediation, regulatory compliance and the provision of legal services for Chinese mainland enterprises going global. Lawyers will also be needed in emerging fields such as AI governance, digital assets, intellectual property, carbon markets, medical products and low-altitude economic activities. In this sense, the plan places professional services within a much wider ecosystem supporting finance, trade, innovation, maritime activities and international cooperation.

Education is the foundation that will enable young people to participate in professional developments. The plan calls for a “future-ready education system”, including stronger AI literacy and the progressive integration of AI into learning, teaching and assessment. Alongside science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics education, it emphasizes the responsible use of technology, biliterate and trilingual capabilities, cross-cultural exchange and a global perspective. Post-secondary education will also be expanded through basic and emerging disciplines, interdisciplinary studies, and collaboration with mainland and overseas academic and research institutions.

The Northern Metropolis University Town gives physical form to the “integrated development of education, technology and talent”. It will bring together talent cultivation, scientific research, the transformation of research outcomes and industry development, supported by joint programs, faculties and laboratories with renowned mainland and overseas institutions. This “industry-academia-research” model, with the support of government and investors, can shorten the distance between study and application, allowing young people to move more readily from the classroom or laboratory into employment and entrepreneurship. Meanwhile, the “Study in Hong Kong” brand can attract high-quality students to pursue their studies or careers here, enriching Hong Kong’s international learning and talent environment.

Green transformation represents another broad field of opportunity. The plan’s vision of a “green and livable city” encompasses zero-carbon energy, energy-efficient buildings, green transport, hydrogen development, waste-to-resources transformation, ecological protection and a carbon trading hub. Importantly, these are not opportunities only for environmental scientists and engineers. Green and sustainable finance, transition finance, disclosure frameworks, carbon markets and international certification will also require expertise in law, accounting, compliance, standards and project management.

The transformation of established industries will widen this scope further. The development of a smart and green port, green maritime fuel bunkering and trading, sustainable aviation fuel, a circular economy and green BRI cooperation can generate opportunities across technology, logistics, financing, insurance, certification and international trade. Green development should therefore not be regarded as a single profession; it is becoming a new dimension of almost every profession. Young people will be not only the long-term beneficiaries of the low-carbon transition, but also the professionals responsible for implementing it.

The plan also broadens the geographical horizons available to young people. It proposes making the Youth Development Summit a flagship event for “international youth exchange and collaboration”, while expanding exchanges, internships and practical experiences. The Greater Bay Area Youth Employment Scheme and the Alliance of Hong Kong Youth Innovation and Entrepreneurial Bases in the Greater Bay Area will facilitate employment, internship and entrepreneurship, while Qianhai and Nansha provide additional platforms for professional practice and business development. These measures can help young people develop a distinctive dual perspective, backed by the motherland and connected to the world.

Beyond these principal areas, the opportunity map is deliberately diverse. AI and robotics, life and health technology, microelectronics, advanced manufacturing, new energy and future industries can create new technological and research careers. Fintech, digital finance, wealth and risk management, intellectual-property financing and high-value-added supply-chain services can renew Hong Kong’s traditional strengths. Cultural and creative industries, sports, tourism, healthcare innovation, social services and public governance offer further avenues for young people with different abilities and aspirations. Enhanced employment support, on-the-job training, funding and incubation services, and a housing ladder intended to promote youth home ownership, can help make these opportunities more accessible.

A plan alone cannot guarantee a result, just as a revision timetable cannot by itself secure a good grade. But without a timetable, it is much harder to know what to prioritize, how to use limited time and whether progress is being made. The five-year plan offers a framework to help Hong Kong and its young people navigate change with clearer direction.

The author is a youth ambassador for the Hong Kong Association for External Friendship.

text:
The aviation sector is responsible for approximately 3% of global emissions.

Decarbonising aviation is notoriously difficult, due to the high costs and advanced technologies required for the sector.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could be a solution to these challenges, which can potentially reduce CO₂ emissions by 80% compared to traditional jet fuel.

Airbus is one of the companies working on aviation decarbonisation, with its Chief Sustainability Officer Julie Kitcher leading the company's strategy.

Ahead of her appearance on the Global Decarbonisation Strategies panel at Sustainability LIVE: The Leadership Summit at Climate Week NYC, Julie shares her insights with Sustainability Magazine.

Please introduce yourself and your role

I’m Chief Sustainability Officer at Airbus. My role is to help embed sustainability across the business, from the way we operate to how we develop the technologies and solutions that can help decarbonise aviation.

Our purpose is to pioneer sustainable aerospace for a safe and united world. That is really our north star when it comes to decision making as a company. The commercial aviation sector as a whole is also embracing decarbonisation, with a target of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

Sustainability is a real responsibility for Airbus. We want to preserve our planet while continuing to bring the connectivity, security and economic development that aerospace provides to society. Climate change is our most material sustainability priority, and that means thinking about adaptation and mitigation together. We need to reduce emissions while also building resilience in the face of a changing climate.

Tell us about your session at Sustainability LIVE NYC

My session is focused on global decarbonisation strategies and, importantly, how organisations can turn ambition into practical action while remaining competitive and resilient.

This challenge has become tougher and more urgent due to this year’s war in the Middle East, which has brought energy price volatility and disruption to energy trade flows.

As sustainability leaders, we are therefore balancing reducing emissions with the other elements of the so-called energy ‘trilemma’, security and affordability. Those three things must be considered together, and that is true across many different sectors. Every industry has its own emissions profile and its own challenges, but there is a huge amount we can learn from each other.

Discuss Airbus' sustainability priorities

I remain incredibly optimistic about the future of aviation. This is an industry that has always made the impossible possible. At the outset of the twentieth century, people believed flight itself would not be possible. Then they questioned whether it could be made safe or accessible to millions of people. Today, our challenge is to decarbonise and I believe we have the innovation, talent and determination to do it.

Climate change remains our biggest priority, and we approach it through the lens of adaptation and mitigation. Aviation plays a vital role in global connectivity and economic development, so we need to continue demonstrating that value while reducing our environmental footprint.

On mitigation, fleet renewal is one of the biggest opportunities available today. The new generation of aircraft are more fuel efficient and therefore produce fewer CO₂ emissions than their predecessors.

Only around 40% of the aircraft flying today are latest generation technology, so there is significant untapped potential.

We are also working on the next generation of aircraft, which will be vital to the decarbonisation of aviation. In the second half of the 2030s, we expect our new single-aisle airliner to begin flying with customers, featuring lighter materials, more efficient wings, and new engine technology. It would reduce emissions and fuel consumption by between 20 and 30% compared with today’s most efficient aircraft. It would also be capable of flying on 100% Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

With a view to the 2040s, we are also working on the world’s first hydrogen-powered fully-electric airliner. This would be a major breakthrough in aviation history.

On adaptation, we need to continue building the resilience of our business. That means thinking about areas such as energy supplies, energy and water consumption and how our operations respond to the physical impact of climate change.

We also recognise that sustainability cannot be viewed in isolation from the realities of today's world. Security, resilience, energy availability and climate change are increasingly interconnected. As I often say, there is no sustainability without security, and no security without sustainability.

Most importantly, Airbus can’t achieve this transition alone. Progress will depend on governments, industry, investors, energy providers and customers all pulling in the same direction.

What is the importance of cross-industry collaboration in decarbonisation?

While industries may have different emissions profiles, the fundamental challenge is remarkably similar. We’re all working towards long-term decarbonisation goals while balancing competitiveness, resilience and growth.

One of the biggest lessons we’ve learned is that innovation alone is not enough. Developing solutions is only part of the challenge and scaling them requires entire ecosystems to move together.

That is particularly true in aviation. Progress depends on coordination between aircraft manufacturers, engine makers, airlines, airports, fuel producers, energy providers and policymakers. Long-term technologies such as hydrogen are a good example. Through our joint venture with MTU Aero Engines to develop hydrogen fuel-cell propulsion systems and our global Hydrogen Hubs programme, which now includes more than 220 partnerships worldwide, we are working across the whole value chain to help create the infrastructure and capabilities that hydrogen-powered aviation will require.

These transformations take time. If you look at solar or wind power 30 years ago, they faced significant challenges and look at where they are today.

There is a saying I often come back to. If you want to go fast, you go alone. If you want to go further, you go together. I’m optimistic that we’ll get there.

How can the aviation sector scale SAF?

The fundamental question is how we stimulate demand, supply and create a supportive regulatory environment at the same time.

Alongside fleet renewal, SAF has the greatest potential for reducing aviation emissions in the near term. Production continues to grow year on year, although not yet at the speed we would like. That doesn’t mean it isn’t developing. It means we need to keep working across the ecosystem to accelerate it.

Airbus is working with partners across the value chain to help do that. Recent examples include our collaboration with Technip Energies, Safran and Tereos to develop a SAF pathway in France, as well as partnerships and co-investment initiatives with airlines including Air Canada and Cathay Pacific.

There is also an important economic dimension to scaling SAF I think is underestimated. A thriving SAF industry will create jobs, support local economies and strengthen energy security.

For example, a recent study we did with ICF found that a domestic SAF industry in Canada could support around 140,000 jobs and contribute C$32 billion to the economy by 2040. It is a strong example of how decarbonisation could create economic value alongside environmental benefits.
